notes: The sources fetched give both the design maximum (3.0 GeV centre-of-mass energy) and a brief push to about 3.1 GeV in November 1974 to study the J/psi; the headline value is the 3.0 GeV design maximum and the 1974 run is a dated phase (the energy-frontier chart then draws the headline as the energy 'as recorded today' at the start of operation).

After 1978 ADONE ran with single beams as a synchrotron-radiation source and a gamma-ray source; photon science is outside the Atlas scope (A26), so those phases are recorded only as dates. Collider running resumed in 1990-1991 for FENICE.
DAΦNE was built inside the ADONE building after the 1993 shutdown (INFN-LNF page).
accelerator:adone.summary_technical: ADONE: e⁺e⁻ storage ring, 105 m, 1.5 GeV per beam (√s up to 3.0 GeV), 12 cells with four experimental straight sections, Varian 350 MeV injector linac; construction from 1963, first electron beam stored end 1967, colliding-beam physics 1969-1978 (Gamma-Gamma, Mu-Pion, Boson, BCF; then Gamma-Gamma 2, MEA, Baryon-Antibaryon), synchrotron-radiation and gamma-ray source from 1978, FENICE 1990-1993; shut down 26 April 1993; the building then hosted DAΦNE.

notes: RHIC, the main current user of this accelerator's beam, completed its final run on 2026-02-06 and is being converted into the Electron-Ion Collider (src:bnl-newsroom-eic-transformation-2026). No source consulted states whether or how AGS operations have changed since; the status 'active' is carried forward from the present-tense official page of 2026-09-17 and should be re-checked once BNL publishes the AGS's post-RHIC operating plan.
No source consulted gives the AGS circumference, so none is recorded under specs.

Injector chain: Linac (200 MeV) to Booster (1.5 GeV protons) to AGS (24 GeV protons, or 8.86 GeV per nucleon for gold) to RHIC. The AGS 'receives protons and other ions from the AGS Booster and delivers them to the Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider after acceleration' (src:bnl-rhic-ags-page).
accelerator:ags.summary_technical: Brookhaven's Alternating Gradient Synchrotron, commissioned in 1960 using the strong-focusing (alternating-gradient) principle invented there; reached a design energy of 33 GeV for protons. Now serves as part of the injector chain that accelerates protons and heavy ions before delivery to the Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider.

accelerator:bepc.summary_technical: BEPC e⁺e⁻ storage-ring collider in the tau-charm energy region: State Council approval April 1983, groundbreaking October 1984, first collisions 16 October 1988; ran 1988-1995, was upgraded and ran again 1998-2004; rebuilt as BEPCII from 2004. Detector: BES (BESI 1989-95, BESII 1998-2004).

notes: The BEPCII-U target parameters (beam energy up to 2.8 GeV, luminosity gains) appear in the IPAC'26 paper tables; they are not recorded as specs because the paper is a preliminary proceedings file.
accelerator:bepcii.summary_technical: BEPCII: two-ring e⁺e⁻ collider, Ecm 2.0-4.2 GeV, design luminosity 1×10³³ cm⁻² s⁻¹ at 1.89 GeV beam energy (reached April 2016); first collisions July 2008 observed by BESIII; shut down 1 July 2024 for an upgrade (BEPCII-U) to raise beam energy and luminosity; machine commissioning from May 2025, design luminosity of the upgraded machine reported achieved on 28 April 2026.

notes: Later history (the Bevalac, 1970s) is not recorded: the Berkeley Lab page that states it returned HTTP 403, so no sourced interval exists for it.
The Bevatron building is not separately geolocated; the accelerator uses the Berkeley Lab campus site.
accelerator:bevatron.summary_technical: Proton synchrotron designed for 6.5 GeV (then written 6.5 BeV), christened the Bevatron when construction was completed in January 1954; operated 1954-1993 at Berkeley Lab. Site of the 1955 antiproton observation.

notes: Source of the energetic heavy-ion beams of the NASA Space Radiation Laboratory (NSRL) as well as the AGS injector; NSRL has no record in the Atlas.

Kinetic energy: the 1.5 GeV is for protons; the heavy-ion energy at Booster extraction is lower per nucleon and is not recorded. A 2023 RHIC review gives "2.3 GeV" for the same stage, apparently a total (not kinetic) energy; the kinetic figure of the Reviews of Modern Physics article is used.
accelerator:bnl-booster.summary_technical: Rapid-cycling booster synchrotron (Building 942) accepting 200 MeV H- ions from the Linac (stripped on injection) or heavy ions from EBIS, accelerating protons to 1.5 GeV kinetic energy for the AGS; also the heavy-ion source for NSRL.

notes: The Linac supplies protons to the Booster and to the Brookhaven Linac Isotope Producer (BLIP); heavy ions come from the Electron Beam Ion Source (EBIS, which replaced the two Tandem Van de Graaffs), neither of which has an accelerator record in the Atlas.
No site is more precise than the Upton campus: the footprint of Building 930 is drawn on the map as a building (approximate).
accelerator:bnl-linac.summary_technical: 200 MeV normal-conducting H- linac (ion sources, RFQ and nine accelerating cavities in a 459 ft tunnel, 135 uA average current); injects the AGS Booster through a charge-exchange foil, and supplies BLIP.

notes: kind is recorded as `linac`; CEBAF is technically a recirculating (racetrack) superconducting linac, which ACCELERATOR_KINDS does not have a dedicated value for.

Eras (2026-10-26, follow-ups 2): the 4 GeV (1995), 6 GeV (2000 to May 2012) and 12 GeV (from 2016) eras are sourced to JLab accelerator papers and the CERN Courier; the 12 GeV Upgrade has its own dated intervals (shutdown and installation May 2012 to December 2013, beam commissioning from December 2013). The 1987 construction start, the 1994 first beam and the 2018 dedication still rest on an encyclopaedia entry (src:jlab-wikipedia) and are unchanged.
accelerator:cebaf.summary_technical: Continuous Electron Beam Accelerator Facility: a superconducting recirculating (racetrack) electron linac at Jefferson Lab; first beam 1994-07-01, design energy of 4 GeV reached in 1995, 6 GeV from 2000 to May 2012, then the 12 GeV Upgrade (shutdown May 2012, beam commissioning from December 2013, first beams to the new Hall D on 7 May 2014, higher-energy experiments since 2016).

notes: The Atlas marker is the IHEP Beijing campus, the laboratory that develops the project, not the tunnel site: the 2023 accelerator TDR describes "forthcoming engineering design phase and site selection procedures", so no tunnel site has been selected.

The accelerator TDR (December 2023) anticipated "Construction is anticipated to begin around 2027-2028, pending government approval, with an estimated duration of 8 years." That schedule is superseded by the October 2025 statement that CEPC will not be in the 2026-2030 plan; no replacement schedule is published in the sources consulted, so no construction interval is recorded.

Study leader Wang Yifang (CERN Courier, 26 October 2025): "We plan to submit CEPC for consideration again in 2030, unless FCC is officially approved before then, in which case we will seek to join FCC, and give up CEPC."
accelerator:cepc.summary_technical: CEPC: proposed e+e- collider in a ~100 km circumference underground tunnel (with a Linac and Damping Ring on the surface and a Booster in the tunnel), 240 GeV Higgs mode, Z mode at 91.2 GeV, WW threshold near 160 GeV, ttbar mode in the TDR; provision for a later SPPC. Pre-CDR 2015, CDR 2018, accelerator TDR 2023 (framework for a forthcoming engineering design phase and site selection), reference-detector TDR October 2025. Not in the 2026-2030 Chinese five-year plan (CERN Courier, 26 October 2025).

notes: accelerator:ps feeds this machine ("A proton beam coming from the PS (Proton Synchrotron) is fired into a block of metal", AD page); that feed edge lives on accelerator:ps, which this stream does not own (listed for the integrator).
accelerator:cern-ad.summary_technical: The AD takes antiprotons produced by a proton beam from the PS striking a metal target and decelerates them, with stochastic and electron cooling, to 5.3 MeV for the AD experiments, now via the ELENA ring. Operating since 2000; in LS3 from 31 August 2026.

notes: CESR continues to operate after 2008 as a synchrotron-light and accelerator-physics facility; photon science is outside the Atlas scope (A26), so this record covers the collider period.
accelerator:cesr.summary_technical: CESR e⁺e⁻ storage ring at the Wilson Synchrotron Laboratory, Cornell: proposal 1975, NSF funding 1977, first electrons April 1979, first colliding-beam luminosity 14 August 1979; Υ region (design 8 GeV beams, 10³² cm⁻² s⁻¹); CLEO at the south and CUSB at the north interaction point; CESR-c (charm threshold) from 2003; CLEO running ended 3 March 2008; ring now used for CHESS and accelerator physics.

notes: The Atlas marker is the CERN Meyrin campus, the host laboratory named by the design report; the CLIC site would be 11 to 50 km long depending on the stage and has no exact location in the sources consulted.
The CERN CLIC page says the collaboration comprises "more than 70 institutes in more than 30 countries".
accelerator:clic.summary_technical: CLIC: proposed normal-conducting two-beam-acceleration linear e+e- collider (12 GHz structures powered by a drive beam), staged at 380 GeV, 1.5 TeV and 3 TeV, site length 11-50 km, hosted by CERN. CDR 2012, Project Implementation Plan 2018 (CERN-2018-010-M). The first stage was costed at about 6 billion CHF with ~170 MW (PIP abstract). No approval is recorded in the sources consulted.

notes: The 1948 AEC approval is quoted in the page but not modelled as an interval, because intervals earlier than 1950 fall before the timeline epoch.
BNL lists the Cosmotron as 1952-1966; the page gives no first-beam date, so the commissioning interval starts at year precision.
accelerator:cosmotron.summary_technical: Proton synchrotron approved by the AEC in April 1948; reached its full design energy of 3.3 GeV in 1953; first synchrotron to provide an external beam; ceased operation in 1966 and was dismantled in 1969.

notes: KLOE start: CERN Courier says KLOE first collected data in 1999; the LNF particle-physics page says it took data from 2000 to 2006.
accelerator:dafne.summary_technical: DAΦNE: two ~100 m e⁺e⁻ rings with two interaction points, √s = 1.02 GeV (φ resonance); first beams 1997, operating from 1999; peak luminosity 2.4×10³² cm⁻² s⁻¹ with the crab-waist scheme; experiments KLOE (1999-2006), FINUDA, DEAR, SIDDHARTA, KLOE-2 (2014-2018), SIDDHARTA-2; also the BTF and DAΦNE-Light.

notes: End of collider running: the DESY DORIS page says ARGUS operated "until 1993"; other sources give end of data taking in 1992. The record follows the DESY page (1993) and marks it approximate.
accelerator:doris.summary_technical: DORIS e⁺e⁻ storage ring, 288 m circumference; two rings up to 3 GeV per beam from 1974 (PLUTO, DASP), single-ring DORIS II from 1982 at up to 5.6 GeV per beam (ARGUS, Crystal Ball), DORIS III from 1991; high-energy-physics running ended 1993, after which it served only as a synchrotron-radiation source.

notes: No design energy or luminosity is recorded: the BNL pages fetched give no numbers (the EIC Yellow Report PDF could not be read as text).
Operations start is not recorded for the collider; the ePIC detector paper of 2023 expected the project detector to start operating in 2032 (see experiment:epic), which may have changed.
The EIC reuses RHIC components (accelerator:rhic), which completed its final run in February 2026; the RHIC record is not edited here.
Status: construction is asserted from the BNL statements that the EIC "is being built" and that RHIC conversion began on 13 April 2026; DOE critical decisions CD-2/CD-3 were not found.
accelerator:eic.summary_technical: EIC: two intersecting accelerators, a polarised electron storage ring and a proton/ion ring (one of RHIC's ion storage rings, its injector chain and its 2.4-mile-circumference tunnel are reused), colliding polarised electron beams with polarised protons and with nuclei from deuterium to uranium; first detector ePIC at the former STAR interaction region. Conversion of RHIC began on 2026-04-13.

accelerator:elena.summary_technical: ELENA decelerates the AD’s 5.3 MeV antiprotons to 0.1 MeV in a 30 m synchrotron with electron cooling, raising trapping efficiency by a factor of 10 to 100. Approved June 2011; first beam tests November 2016; first beam to an experiment October 2018; in LS3 since 31 August 2026.

notes: The Atlas marker is the CERN Meyrin campus, the host laboratory; the proposed ring lies underground beneath CERN and the surrounding regions of France and Switzerland (CERN FCC page).
Status is "proposed": the CERN Council decision on whether to build is planned for 2028 (CERN, 22 May 2026: "the Council will be in a position, by 2028, to take a decision on the FCC-ee").
The FCC programme page also describes a possible later proton-proton stage (FCC-hh); only the electron-positron stage is recorded here.
accelerator:fcc-ee.summary_technical: FCC-ee: proposed 90.7 km circumference e+e- collider in an underground tunnel at 180-400 m depth (200 m average) beneath Haute-Savoie, Ain and the canton of Geneva, the first stage of the FCC programme, which might later be converted to a proton-proton collider. Feasibility Study Report (three volumes, March 2025). European Strategy 2026 update (22 May 2026) recommends FCC-ee as the preferred next flagship at CERN; a Council decision is planned by 2028; if approved: civil engineering 2033-2040, installation after 2038, operation after 2045.

accelerator:fermilab-booster.summary_technical: 474 m circumference rapid-cycling synchrotron running at 15 Hz, accelerating protons from 400 MeV to 8 GeV kinetic energy (8.89 GeV/c) for the BNB and for injection into the Recycler and Main Injector.

notes: The 800 MeV superconducting linac that will replace it (PIP-II, called "Linac2" in Fermilab's May 2026 plan) is accelerator:fermilab-pip-ii.
accelerator:fermilab-linac.summary_technical: 201.25 MHz normal-conducting H- linac delivering 400 MeV to the Booster; to be replaced by the 800 MeV PIP-II superconducting linac.

notes: Design energy 150 GeV per the NuMI beam paper; 120 GeV is the neutrino-production operating point.
accelerator:fermilab-main-injector.summary_technical: 3.3 km circumference proton synchrotron, design energy 150 GeV, operated at 120 GeV for neutrino production; slip-stacked Booster batches are loaded via the Recycler. Source of the NuMI beam and of the future LBNF beam.

accelerator:fermilab-pip-ii.summary_technical: 800 MeV CW-capable superconducting RF H- linac replacing the 400 MeV normal-conducting linac, injecting into the Booster and enabling 1.2 MW of 60-120 GeV protons on the LBNF target.

notes: The Recycler also re-bunches 8 GeV protons for the Muon Campus (Mu2e) and holds beam between the Booster and the Main Injector; the Delivery Ring and the Muon Campus beamlines have no accelerator record in the Atlas.
accelerator:fermilab-recycler.summary_technical: 8 GeV permanent-magnet storage ring in the Main Injector tunnel (3.3 km). Built for Tevatron Run II antiproton storage, now used for Booster-batch stacking and slip stacking ahead of Main Injector acceleration.

notes: Injector chain: Linac (400 MeV) to Booster (8 GeV) to Main Injector (150 GeV, with antiprotons from the Recycler) to Tevatron (980 GeV). Run I (to 1996) was injected by the Main Ring, which has no Atlas record.

Per-run energies (2026-10-26, follow-ups 2): the collider's energy rose from 1.6 TeV (the first collisions, 13 October 1985) to 1.8 TeV (from 30 November 1986, Run 0 and Run I) to 1.96 TeV (Run II, from March 2001); each has its own interval with its centre-of-mass energy, so the view no longer draws the 1.96 TeV of 2001 at 1985. The Run II start was corrected from 2002 to March 2001 (conflict recorded on the interval).
accelerator:fermilab-tevatron.summary_technical: Superconducting proton-antiproton collider, 980 GeV per beam (1.96 TeV centre of mass in Run II, 2002-2011); collider operation from December 1985 to the September 2011 shutdown. Host of CDF and DZero.

notes: Injector chain (Klein & Yoshida 2008, Table 1): protons, RFQ - LINAC III (50 MeV) - DESY III (8 GeV) - PETRA (40 GeV) - HERA (920 GeV); electrons and positrons, LINAC II (450 MeV) - PIA - DESY II (7 GeV) - PETRA (12 GeV) - HERA (27.5 GeV). Only HERA has an Atlas record; the pre-accelerators and PETRA are not linked.

Operation dates: DESY's page says "Research operation: 1992-2007" and Klein & Yoshida say "The first HERA data were taken in summer 1992. It ceased operations in June 2007"; the day (30 June 2007) is from Wikipedia and stays on the interval with its low confidence.

Eras (2026-10-26, follow-ups 2): the cms energy was 300 GeV with 820 GeV protons (1992 to 1998) and 318 GeV with 920 GeV protons (1998 to 2007); the headline 320 GeV is Klein and Yoshida's rounded figure for the second era.
Upgrade of accelerator:lhc.

Sources disagree on the start date: home.cern/science/accelerators/hilumi-lhc says the HiLumi LHC 'should be operational in mid-2030' and src:cern-ls3-farewell-2026 says it is 'scheduled to begin operation in 2030', while ATLAS's own upgrade feature says Run 4 is 'currently planned for 2029'. 2030 is recorded here (two CERN accelerator-side sources); the 2029 date is recorded on experiment:atlas, which is what that ATLAS page describes.
accelerator:hl-lhc.summary_technical: Luminosity upgrade of accelerator:lhc: new Nb3Sn inner triplets, crab cavities, superconducting links and collimation over ~1.2 km, targeting a factor-10 increase in integrated luminosity over the LHC design value; installed during LS3 and scheduled to begin operation in 2030.

notes: The ILC has no site. The Atlas marker is the KEK Tsukuba campus only because an accelerator record needs a facility and a site: KEK hosts the linear-collider workshop LCWS2026 (ILC NewsLine, 17 September 2026). It is NOT a candidate site; the 2013 TDR names Kitakami (Tohoku district, northern Japan) and Sefuri (Kyushu district) as the two possible ILC candidate sites for Asia.
The two detector designs, ILD and SiD, are described in the TDR; they are not recorded as experiments because no host site has been named for them.
The ILC International Development Team was created by ICFA to prepare the ILC Pre-Lab (linearcollider.org); the page fetched does not date its creation.
accelerator:ilc.summary_technical: ILC: proposed superconducting-RF (niobium cavity) linear e+e- collider; TDR (2013) baseline 500 GeV centre-of-mass, extendable to 1 TeV, Higgs-factory mode near 250 GeV, two detectors (ILD and SiD) sharing the luminosity in a push-pull configuration. TDR Vol. 1: two candidate sites for Asia, Kitakami (Tohoku, northern Japan) and Sefuri (Kyushu). No site selected, no approval. The ILC International Development Team (created by ICFA) is to prepare the ILC Pre-Lab.

notes: Per-ring energy: the earlier derived figure (about 31 GeV, half of 62 GeV) is replaced by the sourced 31.4 GeV/c of Bryant (arXiv:1206.3950); CERN's ISR page quotes only the 62 GeV maximum centre-of-mass energy.
accelerator:isr.summary_technical: Two interlaced proton storage rings, each 300 m in diameter, reaching 62 GeV centre-of-mass energy; first hadron collider, operated 1971-1984 and holder of the hadron-collider luminosity record until 2004.

notes: The negative hydrogen ions are converted to protons by charge-stripping foils at RCS injection (T2K instrumentation paper).
accelerator:j-parc-linac.summary_technical: 400 MeV normal-conducting H- linac (324/972 MHz RFQ, DTL, SDTL and ACS), about 300 m long, injecting into the 3 GeV RCS through charge-stripping foils.

notes: Beams leave the main ring by fast extraction to the neutrino beamline (beamline:j-parc-neutrino) and by slow extraction to the Hadron Experimental Facility, which has no beamline record in the Atlas.
accelerator:j-parc-main-ring.summary_technical: 30 GeV fast-extraction proton synchrotron, 1567 m circumference, design beam power ~750 kW, 760 kW reached in December 2023, with an upgrade programme towards 1.3 MW for Hyper-Kamiokande.

accelerator:j-parc-rcs.summary_technical: 3 GeV rapid-cycling synchrotron, about 350 m circumference, 25 Hz repetition, ~1 MW beam power to the Materials and Life Science Experimental Facility; injects into the main ring.

notes: No site is linked: the KEK Tsukuba campus has only the Belle II interaction-region site in the Atlas; the linac building footprint is drawn on the KEK map and linked to this record.

Not recorded: the 1.1 GeV positron damping ring (DR) added for SuperKEKB, the Photon Factory rings (PF and PF-AR) that the linac also injects, and the 12 GeV KEK-PS injector chain (a separate 40 MeV linac and 500 MeV booster).
The linac was originally the Photon Factory electron linac (2.5 GeV); a positron generator for TRISTAN was added and "operated until 1995" (Akai et al.).
accelerator:kek-linac.summary_technical: 600 m electron/positron linac of 60 accelerating units (photocathode RF gun, flux-concentrator positron source, 1.1 GeV damping ring) injecting 7 GeV e- and 4 GeV e+ into SuperKEKB; earlier the 2.5 GeV Photon Factory linac and the 8 GeV / 3.5 GeV KEKB injector.

notes: Located only to campus grade: site:kek-ps-k2k-beamline is the KEK Tsukuba campus point (approximate, precision 1100 m). No source consulted gives the ring's own coordinates.
accelerator:kek-ps.summary_technical: 12 GeV slow/fast-cycling proton synchrotron at Tsukuba, fed by a Cockcroft-Walton, a 20 MeV linac and a 500 MeV booster. Drove the K2K neutrino beamline from 1999 until the end of K2K data taking in November 2004; experiments ended in December 2005.

notes: Construction and commissioning intervals are missing: no fetched source gives KEKB construction start or first-beam dates.
Injected by the KEK electron-positron linac (accelerator:kek-linac), 1998 to 2010.
accelerator:kekb.summary_technical: Asymmetric-energy e⁺e⁻ double-ring collider (8 GeV HER × 3.5 GeV LER) operating on the Υ(4S) resonance, 3 km circumference; peak luminosity 2.11×10³⁴ cm⁻² s⁻¹ with crab cavities, more than 1 ab⁻¹ integrated.

notes: kind is `linac`; LANSCE's proton beam also feeds spallation-neutron and other secondary-beam facilities not modeled here.
accelerator:lansce.summary_technical: Los Alamos Neutron Science Center linac (Technical Area 53), originally LAMPF, opened June 1972; accelerates protons to 800 MeV; its beam-stop neutrinos fed the LSND experiment.

notes: Created because experiment:ps210 (first antihydrogen atoms, 1995) ran on LEAR.
accelerator:lear.summary_technical: LEAR decelerated and stored antiprotons (1982-1996) for fixed-target and internal-target experiments including PS210. Its main magnets were reused for LEIR.

notes: Per-beam energies (≈45.5 GeV at LEP1, ≈104.5 GeV at LEP2) are recorded as derived halves of the sourced centre-of-mass energies; home.cern quotes only the collision energies.

Per-run energies (2026-10-26, follow-ups 2): LEP2's energy rose in steps from 1995 to 2000, so the LEP2 phase carries no energy of its own and each data-taking year or run has its own interval with its centre-of-mass energy (the highest of the energy points of that run) and a derived half per beam. The 209 GeV maximum belongs to 2000 only.
accelerator:lep.summary_technical: 27 km e⁺e⁻ storage-ring collider with four experiments (ALEPH, DELPHI, L3, OPAL). LEP1 ran at the Z pole (~91 GeV cms); after the 1995 upgrade LEP2 reached 209 GeV cms in 2000. Closed 2 November 2000; its tunnel now houses the LHC.

notes: Per-run beam energies are carried on the Interval.specs of each run.
No CERN page consulted states the 2012 increase from 3.5 to 4 TeV per beam; the Run 1 interval therefore records 3.5 TeV/beam with a note.
The LHC occupies the 26.7 km tunnel built for LEP (src:cern-lep-page: 'Its 27-kilometre tunnel now hosts the LHC').
accelerator:lhc.summary_technical: Superconducting proton-proton (and heavy-ion) collider of 26 659 m circumference in the former LEP tunnel; 1232 main dipoles at 1.9 K; design 7 TeV/beam (14 TeV cms) at 10³⁴ cm⁻² s⁻¹; ran at 3.5-4 TeV/beam in Run 1, 6.5 TeV/beam in Run 2 and 6.8 TeV/beam in Run 3.

accelerator:linac2.summary_technical: Proton linac delivering 50 MeV to the PS Booster from 1978 until 12 November 2018; replaced Linac1 and was itself replaced by Linac4.

accelerator:linac4.summary_technical: 86 m H- linac (RFQ to 3 MeV, DTL to 50 MeV, CCDTL to 100 MeV, PIMS to 160 MeV) injecting into the PS Booster; replaced Linac2 during the 2019-20 long shutdown.

notes: kind linac is a stand-in: MAMI is a cascade of racetrack and harmonic double-sided microtrons (a recirculating linac), as the CEBAF record does.
accelerator:mami.summary_technical: Mainz Microtron: three racetrack microtrons in sequence (MAMI B, 855.1 MeV, 90 circulations) followed by a harmonic double-sided microtron (MAMI C, 1508 MeV, 43 circulations), continuous-wave electron beam at 2.45 GHz; operated since the 1980s; recorded as a linac because ACCELERATOR_KINDS has no microtron.

notes: 10 mA (6e16 electrons per second) is the design beam current quoted on the MESA page; it is not recorded as a spec because the A8 current dimension is only accepted in A and mA and the page ties it to the sample hit rate.
accelerator:mesa.summary_technical: Mainz Energy-recovering Superconducting Accelerator: electrons pre-accelerated to 5 MeV by the MAMBO linac enter an energy-recovery linac accelerating them to up to 155 MeV (external-beam mode for P2) with up to 10 mA (6e16 electrons per second); under construction within the PRISMA+ cluster; electron source first beam at the final location on 2024-04-25.

notes: Status commissioning as of 2026-10-26: Run 1 ran from 25 March 2025 to April 2026 and a second run was scheduled for autumn 2026; the 27 August 2026 start of Run 2 comes from a JINR report not fetched here. No source reports recorded beam collisions yet.
The planned and delivered luminosity figures are targets, not achievements.
accelerator:nica.summary_technical: Nuclotron-based Ion Collider fAcility: two superconducting collider rings fed by KRION-6T source, LUTI linac, Booster and Nuclotron; design for heavy-ion collisions (xenon at 2-2.5 GeV/nucleon, luminosity 1e24-1e25 cm^-2 s^-1 targeted in the next run) and polarised p and d collisions up to 27 GeV with luminosity up to 1e32; Run 1 (2025-2026) achieved stable xenon circulation; MPD and SPD are the collider experiments.

notes: The commissioning year (March 1993) is from the 2015 HIAT paper; the modernisation known as Nuclotron-M is part of the NICA project and is not recorded as a separate interval.
accelerator:nuclotron.summary_technical: Nuclotron: superconducting synchrotron (cold-iron fast-cycling magnets) in operation since March 1993, delivering beams from protons to gold ions at 1-6 AGeV (light ions) and up to 4.5 AGeV (heavy ions) to BM@N and, via the Booster chain, to the NICA collider.

notes: The ring and its interaction regions are on the SLAC campus; the PEP site marker is the SLAC campus point. The existing PEP-II record places PEP-II at the IR-2 hall (site:slac-pep-ii-ir2-babar).
accelerator:pep.summary_technical: PEP e⁺e⁻ storage-ring collider at SLAC, 2.2 km circumference, injected by the SLAC linac, centre-of-mass energy about 29 GeV for the experiments recorded here; construction began June 1977, operation 1980-1990; experiments included MAC, PEP-4 (TPC) and Mark II; the ring was reused for the high-energy ring of PEP-II.

notes: Injected by the SLAC linac (accelerator:slac-linac). The earlier version of this record listed accelerator:slac-linac as a downstream machine of PEP-II (a reversed link); it is fixed on the linac record, with the sources of the injection (PAC 1995, WAQ15).
accelerator:pep-ii.summary_technical: PEP-II B-factory: an asymmetric-energy electron-positron collider at SLAC (9 GeV e⁻ × 3.1 GeV e⁺, cms 10.58 GeV, tuned to the Υ(4S) resonance), 2.2 km circumference, feeding the BaBar detector, 1999-2008.

notes: The DESY anniversary page says PETRA served as pre-accelerator for HERA "starting in 1986"; Bethke & Wagner (Eur. Phys. J. H 2022) say PETRA "came back to life in 1990 as PETRA-II" after the November 1986 shutdown. The record follows the latter for the collider/pre-accelerator distinction and only models the collider period.
PETRA II (HERA pre-accelerator) and PETRA III (synchrotron-radiation source) are not separate records here; photon science is outside the Atlas scope (A26).

Feed link to accelerator:hera added 2026-10-26 (follow-ups 2): PETRA II was HERA's pre-accelerator from 1990 to 2007. No source read states a feed relation between DORIS and PETRA: Bethke and Wagner call DORIS and SPEAR "PETRA's precursor e+ e− colliders" (earlier machines, not a stage of the chain), so no link is recorded.
accelerator:petra.summary_technical: PETRA e⁺e⁻ storage-ring collider, 2304 m circumference, beam energy up to 23.39 GeV (centre-of-mass up to about 46.8 GeV); first collisions September 1978, final collider shutdown 3 November 1986. Four collision regions: TASSO, MARK J, JADE and PLUTO (replaced by CELLO in March 1980). Later reused as HERA pre-accelerator and as the PETRA III light source.

accelerator:ps.summary_technical: 628 m proton synchrotron, 277 room-temperature magnets (100 dipoles), top energy 26 GeV; accepts 2 GeV protons from the PS Booster or ions from LEIR and injects into the SPS.

notes: CONFLICT (era of the 1.4 GeV extraction energy): the CERN PSB page says the Booster "received protons from Linac2 at 50 MeV and accelerated them to 1.4 GeV" from 1978 until 2018; CERN Courier (1999) says the Booster energy was raised to 1.4 GeV in 1999, after 800 MeV (1972) and 1 GeV. The Courier dates are used for the 1.4 GeV interval; the PSB page is kept for the 50 MeV Linac2 injection.
accelerator:psb.summary_technical: Four superimposed synchrotron rings; receives 160 MeV H- from Linac4 (stripped to protons on injection) and accelerates to 2 GeV for the PS. From 1978 to 2018 it received 50 MeV protons from Linac2 and delivered 1.4 GeV.

notes: Beam power: the official psi.ch/en/cas/hipa page (checked 2026-09-17) gives 1.4 MW. The 1974 start year is stated by PSI's Ring Cyclotron page and by an official PSI news story (src:facilities-verify-psi-hipa-turns-50: 'went into operation in 1974').

site_id is set to site:bnl-upton-campus (the general BNL campus) rather than either IP-specific site, because RHIC is a ring machine spanning both interaction points and the tunnel between them, not a single point; the campus site is the most representative single location, matching the accelerator's own facility-level coordinate anchor.

Injector chain: Linac (accelerator:bnl-linac, 200 MeV) to Booster (accelerator:bnl-booster, 1.5 GeV) to AGS (accelerator:ags, 24 GeV protons) to RHIC; heavy ions entered the Booster from EBIS and, before that, from the Tandem Van de Graaffs, neither of which has a record.

Eras (2026-10-26, follow-ups 2): Run 1 (2000) at 130 GeV per nucleon pair (65 GeV per nucleon), Run 2 (from July 2001) at 200 GeV (100 GeV per nucleon), then the Run 22 proton-proton energy of 500 GeV. The headline 200 GeV is now a dated value, not drawn at 2000.
accelerator:rhic.summary_technical: Two intersecting 3.86 km (2.4 mi) superconducting storage rings at Brookhaven National Laboratory; the world's first heavy-ion collider and only polarized-proton collider, reaching 200 GeV per colliding gold-gold nucleon pair and up to 500 GeV in polarized proton-proton collisions. Operated 2000-2026 across 25 runs; its final run ended 2026-02-06, after which the machine began conversion into the Electron-Ion Collider (EIC).

notes: The Atlas marker is the BINP campus: the 2018 CDR places the project 'in the Budker Institute of Nuclear Physics (Novosibirsk, Russia)' without a more precise site, so no tunnel site is recorded.

Parameters differ between documents: the 2018 CDR gives 2 to 5 GeV; the BINP project page also 2 to 5 GeV; a 2020 JINST conference paper (arXiv:2005.09878) says 2 to 7 GeV. The record follows the CDR.
accelerator:sctf.summary_technical: SCTF: two-ring e⁺e⁻ collider with crab-waist collisions, full-energy linac and polarised electron injector, √s = 2 to 5 GeV (2 to 7 GeV in a 2020 paper), peak luminosity about 10³⁵ cm⁻² s⁻¹, longitudinally polarised electrons at the interaction point; very preliminary conceptual design report (2 parts) BINP 2018; BINP still described itself as developing the project in 2020. Status after 2020 not found.

notes: Status as of 2026-10-26 from the IPAC 2025 paper (arXiv:2510.14948, October 2025): the first project stage includes the SIS100, the Super-FRS and beam transport lines; "First Science" and "First Science +" stage definitions are not recorded here.
accelerator:sis100.summary_technical: SIS100: superconducting 100 Tm heavy-ion synchrotron (1100 m circumference, tunnel up to 17 m deep) of the first FAIR project stage with the Super-FRS and beam transport lines; injected from the SIS18; installation in the tunnels since early 2024, beam commissioning scheduled for the second half of 2027.

notes: The SIS18 is the GSI ring that the FAIR page says will serve as the first acceleration stage (with the UNILAC) for FAIR.
accelerator:sis18.summary_technical: SIS18: heavy-ion synchrotron (216 m circumference) commissioned in 1990, fed by the UNILAC, delivering ions to speeds of about 0.9c for GSI experiments (HADES) and, in future, injecting the SIS100.

notes: The linac has fed SPEAR (from 1972) and PEP (1980-1990), both linked here since 2026-10-26 (follow-ups 2); PEP-II (1999-2008) is linked here; LCLS has no record. The SLC (1989-1998) did not take beam from the linac: "Starting in 1983, extensive modifications and additions to the existing linac enabled it to simultaneously accelerate and collide 50 GeV electrons and positron bunches" (SLAC handbook page), so the linac was the SLC's accelerator, and no feeds relationship is recorded.
accelerator:slac-linac.summary_technical: The 3.2 km SLAC linear accelerator (operating since 1966), capable of up to 50 GeV for electrons; the accelerator of the Stanford Linear Collider (1989-1998), injector for the PEP-II B-factory (1999-2008), and also feeds the LCLS free-electron laser, which has no accelerator record in the Atlas.

notes: The SLC used the SLAC linac itself as its accelerator, not as an injector ("Starting in 1983, extensive modifications and additions to the existing linac enabled it to simultaneously accelerate and collide 50 GeV electrons and positron bunches on a pulse-to-pulse basis", SLAC handbook page): see accelerator:slac-linac.
accelerator:slc.summary_technical: Stanford Linear Collider: SLAC's linac accelerated electrons and positrons (up to 50 GeV per beam) around a single-pass arc to collide at the Z resonance (~91 GeV cms, ~45.5 GeV/beam), studied by the SLD detector, 1989-1998.

notes: kind is recorded as `linac`; the SNS accelerator complex also includes an accumulator ring, which this record does not model separately.
accelerator:sns.summary_technical: Spallation Neutron Source: a proton linac (1.0 GeV as built, 1.3 GeV since the Proton Power Upgrade) and accumulator ring at ORNL delivering pulsed spallation neutrons from a liquid-mercury target; construction began in late 1999 and the project finished in May 2006, user experiments began in 2008; beam power upgraded from the 1.4 MW design to 2.8 MW capability (Proton Power Upgrade), with the official SNS page of 2026-09-17 reporting 1.8 MW on target.

notes: SSRL describes the tau as "discovered at SPEAR in 1976"; the discovery paper (Mark I, Phys. Rev. Lett. 35, 1489) is dated December 1975, the date used on the result record.
The ring and its detectors are on the SLAC campus; the SPEAR site marker is the SLAC campus point, not the ring.
accelerator:spear.summary_technical: SPEAR e⁺e⁻ storage ring at SLAC: beams up to 4 GeV (about 8 GeV total), 234 m circumference; operations began 1972; detectors Mark I (1973-1977), Mark II (1977-1979), Crystal Ball, Mark III (1981-1988); dedicated to synchrotron-radiation research from 1990 (now SPEAR3).

notes: CONFLICT on the Sp̄pS collider era: home.cern's UA1 page gives 1981-1990 ('It ran from 1981 until 1990, when the SPS was used as a proton-antiproton collider'); some literature extends the era to 1991. The sourced 1981-1990 is recorded.
is_collider is false because the SPS is normally a synchrotron injector; its proton-antiproton collider operation is carried as a separate interval.

The North Area fixed-target beams (beamline:cern-north-area) and the CNGS neutrino beam (beamline:cngs) were extracted from the SPS at 400 GeV/c; the SPS history page says the North Area "took beams of 400 and later 450 GeV".
accelerator:sps.summary_technical: ~7 km proton synchrotron, 1317 room-temperature magnets, top energy 450 GeV; LHC injector and fixed-target source for the North Area, NA61/SHINE, NA62, COMPASS and AWAKE; operated as the Sp̄pS proton-antiproton collider for UA1/UA2 from 1981 to 1990.

notes: The Atlas marker is an area point in Hefei's Future Big Science City: the project talks name the city district as the site (about 1 km²) and show three candidate sites under geological exploration, so no tunnel site has been selected.
The accelerator CDR says construction would 'commence as planned in 2027 or 2028' if approved; that is a plan, recorded here as a note, not as an interval.
Budget figures in the project talks (about 4.5 to 4.98 billion CNY for construction, 364 to 400 million CNY for the key-technology R&D) are not recorded as specs.
accelerator:stcf.summary_technical: STCF: double-ring e⁺e⁻ collider with crab-waist collisions (ring about 860 m, linac injector with damping ring, top-up injection), √s = 2 to 7 GeV, design peak luminosity above 5×10³⁴ cm⁻² s⁻¹ at 4 GeV, optional polarised electron beam; Physics & Detector CDR 2023 (arXiv:2303.15790), accelerator CDR 2025 (arXiv:2509.11522); proposed 2011, key-technology R&D funded by Anhui, Hefei and USTC since 2023; seeking construction in the 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-2030). Not approved in the sources fetched.

notes: Sources disagree on the design luminosity: 8×10³⁵ (2018 accelerator paper and belle2.org) vs 6.0×10³⁵ (2025 Belle II strategy input). The newer value is recorded as the design luminosity and both are quoted.

Injected by the KEK electron-positron linac (accelerator:kek-linac) through the 1.1 GeV positron damping ring; injection energies 7.007 GeV (electrons) and 4.0 GeV (positrons), NIM A 907 (2018) 188, Table 2.
accelerator:superkekb.summary_technical: Asymmetric e⁺e⁻ double-ring collider, 7 GeV HER × 4 GeV LER at √s = 10.579 GeV, 3 km circumference, using the nano-beam scheme with a large crossing angle; target luminosity 6×10³⁵ cm⁻² s⁻¹ (originally 8×10³⁵), peak achieved 5.319×10³⁴ cm⁻² s⁻¹ on 30 June 2026.

notes: Kondo gives "operation 1986-1995" and "data taking 1987-1995"; the KEK history page gives experiments May 1987 to December 1995. The record uses the KEK history page for the operating interval and the 14 November 1986 date for the first collisions.
The original design (1973) was a three-ring electron-proton facility; only the electron-positron main ring was built in phase 1 (Kondo).
accelerator:tristan.summary_technical: TRISTAN e⁺e⁻ main ring (phase 1 of a planned three-ring facility): 3016 m circumference, beam energy 25.5 GeV (1986) rising to 30 GeV (1988, superconducting RF) and 32 GeV; peak luminosity 4.5×10³¹ cm⁻² s⁻¹; approved April 1981, groundbreaking November 1981, first collisions 14 November 1986, experiments May 1987 to December 1995; experiments AMY, TOPAZ, VENUS.

notes: The VEPP-2000 status page (vepp2k.inp.nsk.su/status) read zero beam currents on 23 October 2026; this is a snapshot of the control-system display, not evidence that the collider is decommissioned, and the record follows the 2026 CMD-3 statement that running continues in 2024-2026.
accelerator:vepp-2000.summary_technical: VEPP-2000: e⁺e⁻ collider with the round-colliding-beams concept, c.m. energy 0.3-2.0 GeV, circumference 24.4 m, luminosity 0.8×10³² cm⁻² s⁻¹ achieved at 2 GeV (project 1.0×10³²); construction completed 2007, data taking with CMD-3 and SND from 2010; new injection complex 2013-2016; data taken in 2025 with the beam direction reversed.

notes: The brief names VEPP-2000 and VEPP-4M; VEPP-2M is an addition because CMD-2 and SND ran on it.

Start-date conflict: Skrinsky (1995) "started to operate for experiments at 1975"; Berkaev et al. (2011) "Since 1974"; Shatunov (2018) "VEPP-2M (1972-2000)". The record follows Skrinsky (experiments) and notes the others.
accelerator:vepp-2m.summary_technical: VEPP-2M e⁺e⁻ collider at BINP: centre-of-mass energy range 0.36-1.4 GeV, operating for experiments from 1975 (some sources 1972/1974) to 2000; detectors ND (1982-87), CMD-1, CMD-2 (1992-2000) and SND (1995-2000); modernised into VEPP-2000 after 2000.

notes: The VEPP-4 to VEPP-4M upgrade date is not stated in the sources fetched; the record starts at the VEPP-4 start (1980).
accelerator:vepp-4m.summary_technical: VEPP-4M e⁺e⁻ collider (VEPP-4 complex with the VEPP-3 storage ring and an injector): up to 6 GeV per beam; precise beam-energy measurement by resonant depolarisation (about 10⁻⁷ relative accuracy) and Compton backscattering; operating since 1980 as VEPP-4; KEDR experiments since 2002.

notes: The BNB start date (2002) is not sourced; see the interval note.

Short-baseline detector baselines are not recorded: SBND, MicroBooNE and ICARUS all sit on site:fermilab-main-campus, the same campus point as the beamline, so no site-to-site distance exists. Sourced figures for when separate detector sites exist (SBN proposal, arXiv:1503.01520, src:sbn-proposal-2015): SBND (then LAr1-ND) "will be located 110 m from the BNB target"; MicroBooNE "is located in the Liquid Argon Test Facility (LArTF) at 470 m"; the ICARUS T600 "will be located 600 m from the BNB target". SBND's own detector paper (arXiv:2504.00245) gives "located 110 meters from the Booster Neutrino Beam (BNB) target at Fermilab".
beamline:bnb.summary_technical: On-axis muon-neutrino beam from 8 GeV kinetic (8.89 GeV/c) Booster protons on a beryllium target inside a pulsed horn, mean neutrino energy about 800 MeV, serving MiniBooNE, MicroBooNE, SBND and ICARUS at baselines of order 500 m.

notes: The North Area is a set of beamlines (H2, H4, H6, H8, M2, K12/P42) rather than one line; it is recorded as one beamline fed by accelerator:sps. It is not linked to experiments here (the NA experiments cite accelerator:sps): COMPASS/AMBER, NA61/SHINE, NA62, NA63, NA64 and NA65 are served, per CERN's accelerator-complex page.

Sources differ on the primary energy: the BE-EA page and the Physics Beyond Colliders report give a 400 GeV/c SPS proton beam; the SPS Operations history says "The North Area took beams of 400 and later 450 GeV, both fast- and resonant slow extracted". 400 GeV/c is recorded (current page).
Only site:cern-ecn3-north-area is listed as a detector site (NA62's cavern); EHN1 and EHN2 have no Atlas site record.
beamline:cern-north-area.summary_technical: Slow-extracted 400 GeV/c SPS protons on targets T2, T4 and T6 produce seven secondary and tertiary beamlines (H2, H4, H6, H8 in EHN1; M2 to EHN2; K12/P42 to ECN3). In use since late 1976; shut down with the SPS for LS3 from 31 August 2026.

notes: The CERN end is recorded as site:cern-meyrin, the default CERN site; no more specific sourced coordinate for the CNGS extraction point was found.
beamline:cngs.summary_technical: CERN Super Proton Synchrotron protons directed onto a graphite target to produce a muon-neutrino beam aimed 732 km through the Earth's crust at LNGS; operated July 2006 to December 2012, providing the neutrino source for the OPERA experiment's νμ → ντ appearance search.

beamline:j-parc-neutrino.summary_technical: Fast-extracted 30 GeV protons from the main ring are bent 80.7 degrees towards Kamioka, hit a 91.4 cm graphite target inside three pulsed magnetic horns, and the secondary pions decay in a 96 m helium-filled volume. The resulting narrow-band muon-neutrino beam is measured at 280 m (INGRID on-axis, ND280 off-axis) and at Super-Kamiokande at 2.504 degrees off-axis.

beamline:kek-neutrino.summary_technical: Single-turn extracted 12 GeV protons from the KEK-PS onto a 66 cm long, 3 cm diameter aluminium target inside a two-horn focusing system, followed by a 200 m decay volume and a beam dump; near detectors at about 300 m, Super-Kamiokande at 250 km. Mean neutrino energy about 1.5 GeV.

notes: A dedicated LBNF beam design document is not among the sources; beam parameters come from the DUNE FD TDR Vol. I.
beamline:lbnf.summary_technical: On-axis wide-band muon-neutrino beam from 60-120 GeV Main Injector protons, 1.0-1.2 MW initially and upgradable to 2.4 MW, with a 1285 km baseline from Fermilab to the SURF 4850 Level, together with the far-site conventional facilities.

notes: Near-detector baselines are not recorded: the MINOS, MINERvA and NOvA near detectors all sit on site:fermilab-main-campus, the same campus point as the beamline, so no site-to-site distance exists. Sourced figures for when separate near-detector sites exist: the MINOS near detector is "1040 m from the primary target" (MINOS detector paper, §6.1); the NOvA near detector is "located 1 km downstream of the neutrino production target" (arXiv:2512.20294).
beamline:numi.summary_technical: 120 GeV Main Injector protons on a 1 m graphite target, two magnetic horns and a 675 m decay volume, aimed 58 mrad downward toward Soudan. Served MINOS (2005-2012) and, since September 2013, NOvA (14.6 mrad off axis), MINOS+ and MINERvA.

collaboration:a1-mami.summary_technical: A1 Collaboration (Institut für Kernphysik, JGU Mainz); 19 members listed for 2017 on the A1 website; spokesperson Harald Merkel.

collaboration:a2-mami.summary_technical: A2 Collaboration, an international collaboration based at the Institut für Kernphysik, JGU Mainz; membership counts not published on the pages fetched.

notes: Membership counts not recorded: the member page lists current and former members but was not parsed into a roster.

Institutions named on the collaboration's member page (fetched 2026-10-26): Institut fuer Kernphysik, Johannes Gutenberg-Universitaet Mainz; Petersburg Nuclear Physics Institute (Gatchina); Institut de Physique Nucleaire (IPN) Orsay; Laboratory for Nuclear Science, MIT.
collaboration:a4-mami.summary_technical: A4 Collaboration (Institut fuer Kernphysik Mainz with IPN Orsay, PNPI Gatchina and MIT LNS, as listed on the collaboration's member page); membership counts not recorded.

collaboration:abracadabra.summary_technical: ABRACADABRA Collaboration, MIT-hosted, publishing under that byline through the 2018-2021 axion-search program.

notes: Membership counts left null: no member count was read from a fetched source (no roster fetched).
The official ACT website (act.princeton.edu) returned HTTP 403 to every request, so it is not cited; LAMBDA's ACT overview and the ACT papers are used instead.
collaboration:act.summary_technical: Team behind the Atacama Cosmology Telescope (MBAC, ACTPol, Advanced ACTPol); publishes the ACT data releases (DR4-DR6).

notes: No formation date, membership counts or leadership names are sourced for this collaboration (checked 2026-09-17); see the ADMX experiment record for the sourced run history.
collaboration:admx.summary_technical: Multi-institution collaboration operating the ADMX Gen 2 haloscope at CENPA, University of Washington, managed by Fermilab.

collaboration:adone-baryon-antibaryon.summary_technical: Baryon-Antibaryon Group: Frascati, Naples, Pisa and Istituto Superiore di Sanità (INFN-LNF page); signs the 1974 Phys. Rev. Lett. 33, 1408 paper as 'The Baryon-Antibaryon Group'. Membership list not retrieved.

collaboration:adone-bcf.summary_technical: BCF Collaboration: Bologna, CERN and Frascati (INFN-LNF page). Membership list not retrieved.

collaboration:adone-boson.summary_technical: Boson Group: Frascati, Naples, Pavia and Rome (INFN-LNF page). Membership list not retrieved.

notes: Shared by experiment:adone-gamma-gamma (first generation) and experiment:adone-gamma-gamma-2 (second generation).
collaboration:adone-gamma-gamma.summary_technical: Gamma-Gamma Group: researchers from Frascati and Rome (INFN-LNF page); the group signs the 1974 Phys. Rev. Lett. 33, 1408 paper as 'The Gamma-Gamma Group, Laboratori Nazionali di Frascati'. Membership list not retrieved.

collaboration:adone-mea.summary_technical: MEA Group: researchers from Frascati, Naples, Padua and Rome (INFN-LNF page); signs the 1974 Phys. Rev. Lett. 33, 1408 paper as 'The Magnet Experimental Group for ADONE'. Membership list not retrieved.

collaboration:adone-mu-pion.summary_technical: Mu-Pion Group: Frascati, Rome and Padua (INFN-LNF page). Membership list not retrieved.

notes: The member page marks M. Teshima as spokesperson; no leadership row is written because no person record exists for him.
collaboration:agasa.summary_technical: Collaboration of 29 listed members from the University of Tokyo ICRR, Yamanashi, Saitama, Tokyo Institute of Technology, Osaka City, Chiba, Ehime and other universities and institutes, with the Max-Planck-Institut für Physik; spokesperson M. Teshima (member page, 2007).

collaboration:aleph.summary_technical: Approved by the CERN LEPC on 18 November 1982; about 300 scientists from 25 research centres in nine countries across three continents (CERN Courier retrospective).

notes: CONFLICT/history: the 2008 ALICE detector paper (src:colliders-lhc-alice-detector-jinst-2008) states the collaboration then included 'over 1000 physicists and engineers from 105 Institutes in 30 countries' - the smaller, historical figure at first-collisions time, consistent with a collaboration that grew to ~2000/174/40 by 2022. Both figures are genuine, just from different dates; the more recent (2022) figure is used for the current membership block.
No institution-level member list is recorded in the Atlas for this collaboration.
Leadership is left empty: no page consulted names a current ALICE spokesperson.
collaboration:alice.summary_technical: Collaboration operating experiment:alice at CERN LHC Point 2. Formed 1 March 1993 with the submission of the ALICE Letter of Intent to the CERN LHC Committee; approved February 1997. As of April 2022: almost 2000 members, 174 institutes, 40 countries (home.cern), up from 'over 1000 physicists and engineers from 105 Institutes in 30 countries' at the time of the 2008 detector paper.

collaboration:alps-ii.summary_technical: ALPS Collaboration at DESY; ran ALPS I (2007-2010) and now operates ALPS II (data taking since 2023-05-23).

collaboration:amber.summary_technical: AMBER Collaboration: membership is listed in the CERN Greybook (not read); no count is recorded.

notes: Host: Y2L for AMoRE-Pilot and AMoRE-I, Yemilab for AMoRE-II. No roster was found; the Atlas records no memberships.
collaboration:amore.summary_technical: AMoRE (Advanced Mo-based Rare process Experiment) Collaboration, led from the IBS Center for Underground Physics: officially formed in 2009 with nine institutions from five countries; the 2015 design report counts about 90 researchers from 17 institutions in eight countries, a CUP page about 90 collaborators from 16 institutions in seven countries. It runs AMoRE-Pilot and AMoRE-I (Y2L) and builds AMoRE-II (Yemilab).

collaboration:amy.summary_technical: AMY collaboration: led by S. Olsen (Rochester); physicists from the US, Japan, China and South Korea; the first KEK-based international collaboration (Kondo).

notes: No formation date, roster or member count was found; the Atlas records no memberships for this collaboration.
collaboration:anais.summary_technical: ANAIS (Annual modulation with NaI Scintillators), an experiment developed by the Nuclear Physics and Astroparticles group (CAPA) of the University of Zaragoza at the Canfranc Underground Laboratory. Authors on the ANAIS-112 papers are from CAPA, University of Zaragoza and the Laboratorio Subterraneo de Canfranc. The next project, ANAIS+, is a cryogenic SiPM-readout R&D programme.

notes: The official collaboration page names participating institutions (University of Hawai'i at Manoa (lead), Ohio State University, Washington University in St. Louis, UCLA, University of Kansas, University College London, National Taiwan University, University of Delaware, SLAC, Jet Propulsion Laboratory) but states no total institution/country/scientist count; counts are left null rather than derived by counting the list (forbidden by RESEARCH_AGENT_RULES #4).
No institution-level member list or leadership list is recorded in the Atlas for this collaboration.
collaboration:anita.summary_technical: Collaboration led by the University of Hawai'i at Manoa operating the ANITA balloon payload; named partner institutions include Ohio State, Washington University in St. Louis, UCLA, Kansas, UCL, National Taiwan University, Delaware, SLAC and JPL; no published total membership count was found.

notes: No institution-level member list or leadership list is recorded in the Atlas for this collaboration.
collaboration:antares.summary_technical: International collaboration (created 1996) operating the ANTARES deep-sea neutrino telescope off Toulon, France; approximately 150 engineers, technicians and physicists per the collaboration's own site.

collaboration:apex-jlab.summary_technical: APEX Collaboration (JLab proposals PR-10-009 / E12-10-009; spokespeople Rouven Essig, Philip Schuster, Natalia Toro and Bogdan Wojtsekhowski per the APEX page). No membership count found.

notes: No dedicated ARA collaboration site was found (checked 2026-09-17); WIPAC (UW-Madison) is a named lead institution for ARA's field operations per its own project page. Membership counts not found; left null rather than derived from an author list.
No institution-level member list or leadership list is recorded in the Atlas for this collaboration.
collaboration:ara.summary_technical: Collaboration operating the Askaryan Radio Array near the South Pole; WIPAC (University of Wisconsin-Madison) is a named lead institution for field operations; no published total membership count was found.

notes: No official ArDM website was found (the CERN RE18 page and the LSC experiment page for ArDM could not be located); the LSC page for DArTinArDM is the only official page that mentions the former ArDM detector.
No roster or member count was found; the Atlas records no memberships.
collaboration:ardm.summary_technical: ArDM Collaboration (papers of 2013-2018 list ETH Zurich, CIEMAT and CERN PH/DT authors); developed the detector at CERN as Recognised Experiment RE18 and ran it at LSC as EXP-08-2010. One of the four founding projects of the Global Argon Dark Matter Collaboration. No roster or member count was recorded.

notes: The official collaboration page lists a spokesperson for each side (B. D'Ettorre Piazzoli for the Italian side and C. Zhen for the Chinese side, lists dated 2009 and 2005); no leadership rows are written because no person records exist.
collaboration:argo-ybj.summary_technical: Italian institutes (Lecce, Napoli, Roma Tor Vergata, Roma Tre, Torino, Catania/Palermo, Pavia) and Chinese institutes (IHEP Beijing, Shandong, Southwest Jiaotong, Tibet University, Yunnan, Zhengzhou, Hong Kong); two spokespersons (list dated 2009).

collaboration:argus.summary_technical: ARGUS collaboration at DORIS II (DESY); institute list not retrieved.

notes: Hosted at UC Irvine per the official site's own domain/publisher metadata; no total membership count was found.
No institution-level member list or leadership list is recorded in the Atlas for this collaboration.
collaboration:arianna.summary_technical: Collaboration (hosted at UC Irvine) that operated the ARIANNA pilot radio-detection array on the Ross Ice Shelf, now decommissioned; no published total membership count was found.

notes: Sizes from three official ATLAS pages, read 2026-10-25. The collaboration page (atlas.cern/Discover/Collaboration) says 'over 5500 members and 3000 scientific authors', '170+ Institutions', '40 Countries'. The official institutions list (atlaspo.cern.ch/public/institutions) counts 175 institutions, 246 institutes and 40 countries. collaboration:atlas.summary_technical: Collaboration operating experiment:atlas at CERN LHC Point 1. Founded 1 October 1992 with the submission of the ATLAS Letter of Intent to the LHC Experiments Committee. Governed by a Collaboration Board that elects the Spokesperson for renewable two-year terms.

notes: No institution-level member list or leadership list is recorded in the Atlas for this collaboration.

Both are recorded; `formation` uses the INSPIRE value as the more precisely dated of the two, with this note flagging the earlier informal start.
collaboration:babar.summary_technical: International collaboration operating the BaBar detector at the SLAC PEP-II B-factory; per the INSPIRE experiment record, more than 500 scientists, engineers and graduate students from 10 countries.

collaboration:baikal-gvd.summary_technical: Collaboration operating the Baikal-GVD underwater neutrino telescope, led by INR RAS with JINR Dubna and other partners; membership counts not published on the sources consulted.

collaboration:baksan-underground-scintil.summary_technical: Laboratory of the Baksan Neutrino Observatory, INR RAS (with the Institute of Astronomy RAS on the neutrino-burst papers); scientific leadership per the INR page: G. T. Zatsepin and S. P. Mikheev.

collaboration:zeus.summary_technical: International collaboration operating the ZEUS detector at DESY HERA; per the ZEUS collaboration's own site (2007), about 450 physicists.

detector:a1-mami.summary_technical: A1 three-spectrometer setup: spectrometers of about 15 m and more than 200 t each, momentum resolution better than 0.01%, time resolution of 0.5 ns, vertical drift chambers, scintillators, Cherenkov counters, focal-plane polarimeter; plus the KAOS spectrometer.

detector:a2-mami.summary_technical: Crystal Ball (highly segmented NaI(Tl) ball) with the TAPS detector as a forward wall and a central tracker: geometrical acceptance close to 4 pi with good energy and angular resolution, especially for neutral final states; frozen-spin butanol targets after the MAMI-C upgrade.

detector:a4-mami.summary_technical: A4: total-absorption PbF2 Cherenkov calorimeter (1022 crystals in 7 rings, energies summed over clusters of nine crystals, event rate about 100 MHz), 10 cm liquid-hydrogen target, luminosity monitors and microwave-resonator beam monitors, used at forward (30-40 degree) and backward (140-150 degree) angles.

detector:abracadabra.summary_technical: Small-scale (10 cm) toroidal lumped-element / broadband-resonant axion haloscope prototype at MIT; completed its dedicated axion dark-matter search program around 2021 after a 1-month first run (2018) and a broadband final run.

detector:act.summary_technical: 6 m off-axis Gregorian telescope on Cerro Toco (5190 m): MBAC (148/218/277 GHz, 2008-2010), ACTPol (2013-2016) and Advanced ACTPol (2016-2022, 20-280 GHz); decommissioned after final data in 2022.

detector:admx.summary_technical: Tunable copper-plated microwave cavity haloscope inside a superconducting solenoid, cooled by a dilution refrigerator to ~90 mK and read out with near-quantum-limited amplifiers, at CENPA (University of Washington).

detector:adone-baryon-antibaryon.summary_technical: Baryon-Antibaryon detector: large liquid scintillators, wire chambers with magnetostrictive reading, flash tube chambers.

detector:adone-bcf.summary_technical: BCF detector: scintillation counters and spark chambers; the INFN-LNF page stresses its calibration for particle identification.

detector:adone-boson.summary_technical: Boson detector: scintillators and wire magnetostrictive chambers; Frascati, Naples, Pavia and Rome. The INFN-LNF page says its place was later taken by the Naples 'proton-antiproton' experiment.

detector:adone-gamma-gamma.summary_technical: Gamma-Gamma detector: scintillation counters, lead converters and spark chambers; Frascati and Rome group.

detector:adone-gamma-gamma-2.summary_technical: Gamma-Gamma 2 detector: scintillation counters, converters and spark chambers; larger solid angle and better sampling of electromagnetic and hadronic showers.

detector:adone-mea.summary_technical: MEA detector: large gap chambers and spark chambers in a large solenoidal magnet, built because a complete analysis of the final states required a detector in a magnetic field.

detector:adone-mu-pion.summary_technical: Mu-Pion detector: scintillators, spark chambers viewed by long mirrors, water Cerenkov counters, large iron shields interleaved with spark chambers for muon identification, flash tube chambers.

detector:aegis.summary_technical: Two parallel Penning-Malmberg traps in a cryostat and 1 T field for antiproton and positron manipulation, laser-excited Rydberg positronium, and a moire deflectometer with a position-sensitive detector.

detector:agasa.summary_technical: AGASA: 111 plastic-scintillator surface detectors (2.2 m2 each) at about 1 km spacing, 27 muon detectors under absorbers (0.5 GeV muon threshold), optical-fibre data links, central computer control; covered about 100 km2.

detector:aleph.summary_technical: General-purpose LEP detector: silicon-microstrip vertex detector (two double-sided layers), an 8-coordinate inner drift chamber with trigger, a 4.4 m × 3.6 m time projection chamber, electromagnetic and hadron calorimeters, and a 6.3 m × 5.3 m superconducting coil providing a 1.5 T field.

notes: specs.total_mass/length/diameter reflect the as-built (2008) detector; the ALICE 2 upgrade (2021) replaced the ITS and TPC internals but no source consulted gives updated overall mass/dimension figures, so the original detector-paper values are kept with a note.
Placed at site:cern-point-2-alice, whose coordinate is an approximate geocoder-derived campus point (see that record's notes) rather than a surveyed cavern coordinate.
The detector record carries the same Long Shutdown 3 interval and status as experiment:alice, so that the two agree.
detector:alice.summary_technical: General-purpose heavy-ion detector: six-layer silicon Inner Tracking System, cylindrical Time-Projection Chamber, TOF/HMPID/TRD particle-identification arrays and PHOS/EMCal calorimeters inside the 0.5 T L3 solenoid (reused from LEP), plus a forward muon spectrometer (2-9 degrees) with a dipole magnet and 14 tracking/trigger chamber planes. Upgraded (ALICE 2: new ITS2 pixel tracker, GEM-based continuous-readout TPC) for LHC Run 3.

detector:alpha.summary_technical: ALPHA 1 (2005-2012), ALPHA 2 (2012-) and ALPHA 3 (2021-): Penning-Malmberg traps for antihydrogen synthesis with a superposed neutral-atom minimum-B trap, laser access for spectroscopy and laser cooling.

notes: Hall for ALPHA-g is an assumption flagged on the placement: the official page lists the apparatus but not its hall.
detector:alpha-g.summary_technical: ALPHA-g: vertical double Penning-Malmberg and neutral-atom trap, about twice the size of ALPHA 2/3, built to measure the gravitational acceleration of antihydrogen released from magnetic confinement; operating since 2021.

detector:alps-ii.summary_technical: Light-shining-through-a-wall (LSW) apparatus reusing decommissioned HERA superconducting dipole magnets and optical build-up/regeneration cavities at DESY, operating since 2023-05-23.

detector:amber.summary_technical: Upgraded COMPASS two-stage magnetic spectrometer in EHN2, equipped with liquid hydrogen/helium targets, with measurement-specific instrumentation (and, for some proposals, a dedicated target spectrometer with tracking and electromagnetic calorimetry).

detector:amore-i.summary_technical: 13 48depl-Ca100MoO4 + 5 Li2 100MoO4 crystals (6.2 kg) with MMC readout at ~12 mK in the A5 tunnel of Y2L (700 m); full 18-crystal DAQ December 2020 - April 2023 at 93% live time; exposure 8.02 kg yr (3.89 kg yr of 100Mo), background 0.025 +/- 0.002 counts/keV/kg/yr near Q; T1/2(0vbb, 100Mo) > 2.9e24 yr (90% C.L.), m_bb < 210-610 meV.

detector:amore-ii.summary_technical: Array of 423 Li2 100MoO4 crystals (about 90 kg of 100Mo) as MMC-read cryogenic calorimeters in a dilution refrigerator (Leiden, three pulse tubes) with 26 cm lead, boric-acid rubber, 70 cm polyethylene and a water-Cherenkov and plastic-scintillator muon veto, in the AMoRE Hall of Yemilab (about 1,000 m); target background 1e-4 counts/keV/kg/yr, sensitivity T1/2 ~ 6e26 yr (m_bb 15-29 meV, the whole inverted-hierarchy region). Status: under construction; 'upcoming' in July 2026.

detector:amore-pilot.summary_technical: Six 48depl-Ca100MoO4 crystals (1.9 kg total), phonon and scintillation readout with metallic magnetic calorimeters at mK temperatures (dilution refrigerator), in the A5 area of Y2L (700 m). First results from 111 kg d: T1/2(0vbb, 100Mo) > 9.5e22 yr (90% C.L.); a later background study sets T1/2 >= 3.0e23 yr.

detector:amy.summary_technical: AMY: 3 tesla superconducting solenoid (IEEE Trans. Magn. 23 (1987) 520); barrel electromagnetic shower counter (NIM A317 (1992) 75).

detector:anais-112.summary_technical: Nine NaI(Tl) modules of 12.5 kg (Alpha Spectra Inc.), 3x3 matrix, read by photomultipliers, Mylar window for low-energy calibration, light collection of about 15 photoelectrons per keV; hut in hall B of the LSC (2450 m.w.e.).

notes: Placement caveat repeated here from experiment:anita: the launch site is not the detection location.
detector:anita.summary_technical: Balloon-borne quad-ridged horn antenna array for Askaryan-effect radio detection of UHE neutrinos and cosmic rays, flown at ~37 km altitude over Antarctica across five flights (2003-2016), launched from the NASA LDB facility near McMurdo Station.

detector:annie-detector.summary_technical: Instrumented tank with 25 t Gd-loaded water as neutrino target and neutron tagger, 8-inch PMTs plus LAPPDs, a front veto against dirt-induced events and an iron-scintillator muon range detector; located in the SciBooNE hall.

detector:antares.summary_technical: 12-line, 885-OM deep-sea water-Cherenkov neutrino telescope, ~0.02 km³ instrumented volume, at 2475 m depth off Toulon, France. Operated from first-line deployment (2006-02-14) to switch-off (2022-02-12).

detector:apex-jlab.summary_technical: Hall A High Resolution Spectrometers configured at minimum opening angle with septum magnets directing the outgoing e+ and e- into the two arms; gas Cherenkov detectors and timing separate electrons from pions; thin tantalum target.

detector:ara.summary_technical: 5 autonomous ARA in-ice radio stations, 100-200 m deep, deployed 2012-2018 near the South Pole; only A3 and A5+PA (with its low-threshold phased array) confirmed actively collecting data as of the 2024 collaboration overview paper.

detector:ardm.summary_technical: Double-phase liquid argon TPC (scintillation S1 plus ionisation S2 read out through PMT arrays) with an 850 kg active target in a vessel filled with nearly 2 t of LAr; installed in Hall A of LSC (about 2500 m w.e.) in 2013. Run I (2015) was single phase: attenuation length of the argon scintillation light close to 0.5 m, 39Ar activity and Rn-222 emanation measured, and a pulse-shape rejection power for electron recoils above 10^8 estimated with a Cf-252 source (50% nuclear-recoil acceptance, >50 photons). A dual-phase run finished by early 2020. The cryostat is reused by DArTinArDM (Exp-13-2019).

detector:argo.summary_technical: Next-generation argon detector under development by GADMC: 400 t of low-radioactivity underground argon (300 t fiducial) viewed by digital silicon photomultipliers (about 250 m^2), single-phase or dual-phase TPC depending on DarkSide-20k results, in a vacuum cryostat with a water shield; goal of fewer than one background event in the WIMP region over ten years (3000 t yr). Design studies in the SNOLAB Cube Hall (Geometry B); the 2025 SNOLAB report plans construction in the late 2030s, preceded by the ARGOlite prototype (about 2028-2031). No approval or funding decision was found.

detector:argo-ybj.summary_technical: Full-coverage RPC carpet (~78 × 74 m2, 18,480 pads of 56 × 60 cm2, 6 cm strips) with 0.5 cm lead converter and a partially instrumented guard ring to about 100 × 100 m2; time resolution about 1.8 ns.

notes: Run statistics: "The first neutrino candidate was recorded on May 27, 2009."
detector:argoneut-detector.summary_technical: Liquid-argon TPC with 47 cm horizontal drift, three wire planes (two instrumented, induction and collection), a cryostat with a cryocooler re-liquefaction and purification loop; muons exiting are ranged in the MINOS near detector.

detector:argus.summary_technical: ARGUS: a universal detector at DORIS II (NIM A275 (1989) 1-48).

detector:arianna.summary_technical: ARIANNA Hexagonal Radio Array: surface radio-detection stations on the Ross Ice Shelf, from a single 2009 prototype to a 7-8 station pilot array (2014-2019), now decommissioned.

detector:asacusa.summary_technical: Antiprotonic-helium laser-spectroscopy setup and a CUSP superconducting-magnet antihydrogen source with microwave cavity and detector for in-flight hyperfine spectroscopy.

detector:athena.summary_technical: Penning-trap apparatus with a cryogenic mixing region and a position-sensitive annihilation detector, used for the first cold-antihydrogen production in 2002.

notes: CONFLICT on the overall length: the 2008 JINST detector paper says 'The dimensions of the detector are 25 m in height and 44 m in length', while atlas.cern ('46m long') and home.cern ('At 46 m long, 25 m high and 25 m wide') say 46 m. The 46 m value from the collaboration's own current page is recorded in specs.length; the 44 m JINST value is kept in the note of that quantity. The most likely explanation is that the two figures count the forward shielding differently, but no source consulted says so.

CONFLICT on the toroid field: atlas.cern's magnet page says the toroids 'provide a magnetic field of up to 3.5 Tesla' in its text and lists '4 T magnetic field on superconductor' in its barrel- and end-cap-toroid tables. 3.5 T is recorded as the delivered field and 4 T is noted as the peak on the conductor.
Trigger numbers are the 2008 design values from the JINST paper; atlas.cern's current Trigger & DAQ page quotes up to 100 000 events/s after the first level and ~1000 events/s to storage.
detector:atlas.summary_technical: General-purpose 4π collider detector: silicon pixel + SCT + TRT inner detector in a 2 T solenoid, liquid-argon EM and forward calorimetry, scintillator-tile hadronic calorimeter, and an air-core toroid muon spectrometer. Calorimetry to |η| = 4.9, precision tracking to |η| < 2.5, muon measurement to |η| < 2.7.

detector:atrap.summary_technical: Penning-Ioffe trap apparatus using cold positrons to cool antiprotons to form antihydrogen, with annihilation detectors.

detector:babar.summary_technical: General-purpose PEP-II detector: multi-layer silicon vertex tracker inside a cylindrical wire drift chamber, a DIRC ring-imaging Cherenkov particle-identification detector, a CsI crystal electromagnetic calorimeter inside a superconducting solenoid, and resistive-plate-chamber muon/neutral-hadron detectors in the magnet's steel flux return.

detector:baikal-gvd.summary_technical: Modular underwater water-Cherenkov array in Lake Baikal; clusters of 8 strings x 36 OMs deployed annually since 2016; 3456 OMs on 96 strings as of the winter 2023 campaign; lakebed depth ~1366 m; already-deployed clusters have taken continuous physics data since 2018.

detector:baksan-underground-scintillatio.summary_technical: Aluminium tanks (0.7 x 0.7 x 0.3 m^3) of white-spirit scintillator with PPO and POPOP, one 15 cm PMT each; four horizontal and four vertical layers in a concrete-block building; time-of-flight direction measurement (2 ns) separates upward from downward muons.

detector:base.summary_technical: Four-Penning-trap system (analysis trap with a magnetic bottle for spin detection, precision trap, cooling trap, reservoir trap holding 50-100 antiprotons) with image-current detection; the transportable trap BASE-STEP is a separate development.

notes: Subsystem list and dimensions are EMPTY on purpose: the Belle detector paper (NIM A 479 (2002) 117) is paywalled at Elsevier and blocked to automated fetching, and only its title, abstract fragment, DOI and journal reference could be read (via the INSPIRE literature record). Subdetector names (SVD, CDC, ACC, TOF, ECL, KLM) and geometry must be added from the paper itself.
The 1.5 T solenoid field is the only spec taken from a fetched source.
detector:belle.summary_technical: General-purpose 4π spectrometer at the KEKB Tsukuba interaction region, built around a 1.5 T superconducting solenoid with an instrumented iron flux return, optimised for time-dependent CP-violation measurements in B decays.

notes: Overall dimensions other than the 8 m height quoted at the 2017 roll-in are not recorded: only the abstract page of the Belle II Technical Design Report (arXiv:1011.0352) was consulted, so no TDR geometry table is cited. Height: 'the entire 8 m-tall, 1400 tonne Belle II detector system' (belle2.jp, roll-in article); it is quoted here rather than recorded as a spec.
Per-subsystem quantities (channel counts, radii, crystal counts) are unresolved for the same reason.
detector:belle-ii.summary_technical: General-purpose 4π spectrometer at the SuperKEKB interaction point: PXD, SVD, CDC, TOP and ARICH, ECL inside a 1.5 T solenoid, and the KLM in the instrumented flux return; about 1400 t, rolled in on 11 April 2017.

detector:bes.summary_technical: BESI: central drift chamber inside a main drift chamber, electromagnetic calorimeter of self-quenching streamer tubes interleaved with lead.

detector:bes-ii.summary_technical: BESII: revamped MARK II vertex detector replacing the BESI central drift chamber, new main drift chamber and barrel TOF system.

detector:bes-iii.summary_technical: BESIII: helium-based multilayer drift chamber (MDC), plastic-scintillator TOF, CsI(Tl) electromagnetic calorimeter, all inside a superconducting solenoid (1.0 T; 0.9 T in 2012), octagonal steel flux-return yoke with resistive plate counter muon modules; 93% acceptance over 4π; momentum resolution 0.5% at 1 GeV/c; end-cap TOF upgraded in 2015 with MRPCs.

detector:bicep-array.summary_technical: Four BICEP3-class receivers (550 mm aperture) at 30/40, 95, 150 and 220/270 GHz with over 30,000 detectors at the South Pole; first receiver observing since early 2020; replaced the Keck Array.

detector:bicep1.summary_technical: Two-lens refracting telescope with 49 pairs of horn-coupled polarization-sensitive bolometers at 100 and 150 GHz, on a 3-axis mount in the Dark Sector Laboratory; observed 2006-2008, mapping about 2% of the sky.

detector:bicep2.summary_technical: All-cold 26 cm aperture refractor with 512 antenna-coupled TES bolometers at 150 GHz in the Dark Sector Laboratory; observed 2010-2012 over 380-400 deg^2.

detector:bicep3.summary_technical: Compact two-lens refractor, 520 mm aperture, 20 tiles (2560 TES bolometers) at 95 GHz, on the former BICEP1/BICEP2 mount in the Dark Sector Laboratory; science observations since 2016.

detector:bmn.summary_technical: BM@N forward spectrometer (1.6 < eta < 4.4): SP-41 analysing magnet (3.15 Tm at 2000 A), beam and trigger detectors, silicon and GEM tracking, drift/cathode-strip chambers, TOF400/TOF700 walls, calorimetry.

detector:borexino.summary_technical: Liquid-scintillator (pseudocumene+PPO) detector, 278 t active mass, ~100 t fiducial mass, in a nylon vessel with a water-Cherenkov muon veto; operated at LNGS Hall C from May 2007 to October 2021.

detector:boss-spectrographs.summary_technical: Two rebuilt SDSS spectrographs (red and blue cameras split near 6000 Å), 1,000 fibres per plug plate for BOSS and eBOSS, resolution about 1560–2650, 3600–10,400 Å; in SDSS-V one remains at Apache Point and one is at Las Campanas.

detector:brahms.summary_technical: BRAHMS: forward and mid-rapidity magnetic spectrometer arms with particle identification, movable in angle, plus global multiplicity and centrality detectors; specifications not recorded (detector paper unavailable as text).

detector:bugey-detector.summary_technical: Three identical 600 l segmented detectors of 98 prismatic cells viewed by 3-inch PMTs on each side, filled with 6Li-loaded (0.15 %) liquid scintillator; pulse-shape discrimination separates neutron-capture products from positrons.

detector:bullkid-dm.summary_technical: Stack of 16 diced silicon wafers (about 2300 dice, 800 g in total) sensed by multiplexed phonon-mediated kinetic inductance detectors on a thin common disk; segmentation gives fiducialisation and background veto; cryogenic scintillating veto under development.

detector:c-4.summary_technical: Design for four identical p-type point-contact germanium detectors (up to ~1.3 kg each, ~4.1 kg total) in one low-background shield with a plastic-scintillator veto, in the proton-decay hall of Soudan (2800 m.w.e. quoted), aiming at ~0.5 keVee thresholds, ~5x lower background than CoGeNT and sensitivity to ~1e-42 cm^2 at 10 GeV/c^2 after 8 months.

detector:candles-detector.summary_technical: 96 CaF2 modules (10 cm cubes, 3.18 kg each) with wavelength-shifter layers in six layers of 16 in an acrylic LS vessel (1.4 m diameter and height), in a 3 m x 4 m water tank; 62 PMTs (20, 13 and 10 inch); cancellation coils for the Earth's field; pulse-shape discrimination of internal backgrounds.

notes: The first telescope T1 (the former CANGAROO-II) was not in use at the time of the 2007 observations (arXiv:0908.1610).
detector:cangaroo-iii.summary_technical: Four 10 m imaging atmospheric Cherenkov telescopes (114 FRP mirror segments, 57.3 m2, 427-pixel cameras) arranged in a diamond; first telescope the upgraded CANGAROO-II (March 2000), T1 later out of use.

notes: Magnet field (9 T) and length (10 m) are taken from the description field of the already-cited INSPIRE experiment record (checked 2026-09-17).
detector:cast.summary_technical: Straight, twin-bore prototype LHC dipole magnet (formerly LEP DELPHI cryogenics) tracking the Sun, coupled to X-ray optics and detectors for the axion helioscope technique; data-taking 2003-06-18 to 2022-12-31.

detector:cbm.summary_technical: CBM: low-mass radiation-hard detector subsystems for vertexing, tracking, particle identification and event reconstruction with a free-streaming self-triggered readout at up to 10 MHz.

detector:ccfr-detector.summary_technical: Unmagnetised steel-scintillator target calorimeter (690 t, hadronic resolution 0.85/sqrt(E)) instrumented with drift chambers for muon tracking, followed by a solid-iron toroidal spectrometer (dp = 0.11 p); in 1996-97 reused by NuTeV.

detector:ccm-detector.summary_technical: Cylindrical stainless-steel cryostat (2.58 m diameter, 2.26 m height) holding 10 t of LAr, about 3 t active veto and about 5 t (CCM120) / 7 t (CCM200) fiducial volume; 200 8-inch PMTs, 50 % photocathode coverage, 2 ns timing resolution; TPB-coated foils and PMTs (80 % coated) for wavelength shifting.

detector:cdex-1.summary_technical: p-type point-contact germanium (pPCGe) detector, 994 g crystal (CDEX-1A) then CDEX-1B, at CJPL (>2400 m rock). First limit from 14.6 kg d with a 400 eVee threshold; later 737.1 kg d at 160 eVee; a 3.2 yr annual-modulation analysis excludes the DAMA/LIBRA and CoGeNT modulation regions at >99.99% and 98% C.L. in the standard halo model.
