facility:hanford-site.summary_technical: Hanford Site, southeastern Washington: nine nuclear reactors along the Columbia River, plutonium production 1943-1989, cleanup since 1989. Host of the first Cowan-Reines reactor-antineutrino attempt (spring 1953, a 300 L liquid-scintillator detector at one of the Hanford Engineering Works reactors).

notes: The HIGRO name is taken from the HAGAR paper ("first phase of the HImalayan Gamma-Ray Observatory (HIGRO) project") and the MACE sensitivity paper.
No operator is recorded: HAGAR was built by TIFR, IIA, BARC and SINP (author affiliations, Astrophys. Space Sci. Trans. 7, 501) and MACE by BARC; no source fetched names one operator of the site.
The Indian Astronomical Observatory (IIA optical telescopes) is also at Hanle; it is a separate facility and is not recorded here.
facility:hanle-observatory.summary_technical: Hanle (Ladakh, Himalayas, 4270 m a.s.l.): the Himalayan Gamma-Ray Observatory (HIGRO) site, hosting the HAGAR wavefront-sampling array (first phase, regular observations since September 2008) and the 21 m MACE imaging Cherenkov telescope.

notes: operator/operator_text left null: no fetched source names a distinct legal operator.
facility:hess-khomas-highland.summary_technical: H.E.S.S. observatory site on Farm Göllschau in the Khomas Highland, Namibia, at 1800 m altitude, approximately 100 km south-west of Windhoek.

facility:ihep-beijing.summary_technical: IHEP, established February 1973 from Division One of the Institute of Atomic Energy; main campus on Yuquan Road, Beijing, home of BEPC/BEPCII (e⁺e⁻, 2.0-4.2 GeV tau-charm region) with the BESIII detector and the BSRF.

notes: Host facility of the Ricochet experiment.

ILL is primarily a multinational neutron-science user facility; it is recorded here as a reactor site because the property relevant to Ricochet's CEvNS program is its 58 MW (thermal) research reactor core, as for the other CEvNS reactor facilities (Brokdorf, Leibstadt).
facility:ill-grenoble.summary_technical: Institut Laue-Langevin (ILL), Grenoble, France: research reactor of 58 MW thermal power (ILL's own reactor page; Ricochet's own background paper also gives 58 MW); hosts the Ricochet CEvNS experiment 8.8 m from the reactor core.

notes: The facility record stands for the underground site in its role as the IMB host; the mine itself is a commercial salt mine that predates and outlives the experiment, and the APS release does not give a mine opening date.
Status decommissioned means the physics programme ended in 1991, not that the mine closed.
facility:imb-fairport-mine.summary_technical: Fairport Harbor Morton Salt Mine, Ohio: site of the Irvine-Michigan-Brookhaven (IMB) water Cherenkov detector, the first kiloton-scale nucleon-decay detector, 1982-1991, at 1570 m.w.e.

facility:infn-lnf-frascati.summary_technical: INFN-LNF, Frascati (Rome); electron synchrotron (1959), AdA (1961), ADONE (1969) and DAΦNE (a φ-factory e⁺e⁻ collider at 1.02 GeV centre-of-mass energy), with the Beam Test Facility and SPARC_LAB.

notes: Facility record at the level needed for the Troitsk nu-mass experiment; it is not a full record of INR RAS.
facility:inr-troitsk.summary_technical: INR RAS facility at Troitsk hosting the Troitsk nu-mass tritium beta-decay programme (windowless gaseous tritium source, integrating electrostatic spectrometer).

notes: Created by the accelerator-neutrino-historical lead solely to host the placement of experiment:karmen; this record does not attempt full coverage of ISIS's neutron/muon science programme.

ISIS is a pulsed spallation neutron and muon source at the Rutherford Appleton Laboratory operated by STFC; KARMEN used its 800 MeV proton beam stop as a neutrino source (see src:karmen-prc-1998-nue-nutau-limits: 'the beam stop neutrino source ISIS').
facility:isis-neutron-source.summary_technical: STFC-operated pulsed spallation neutron and muon source at the Rutherford Appleton Laboratory, Harwell Campus, Didcot, Oxfordshire, using an 800 MeV proton synchrotron; its beam stop supplied stopped-pion/muon-decay neutrinos to the KARMEN experiment from 1990 to 2001.

notes: The English "What is J-PARC" page (j-parc.jp/en/jparc.html) is older than the current facility pages: it gives the linac as "400 MeV (currently operating at 180 MeV)" and the main ring as "50 GeV (currently 30 GeV)".
facility:j-parc.summary_technical: Accelerator complex at Tokai, Ibaraki: a 400 MeV linac, a 3 GeV rapid-cycling synchrotron and a 30 GeV main ring, feeding the Materials and Life Science, Hadron and Neutrino experimental facilities. The neutrino facility drives T2K and will drive Hyper-Kamiokande.

notes: No official JUSL page was found; the laboratory is known here only from the InDEx papers. Overburden in m.w.e. and the operating body are unresolved.
facility:jaduguda-underground-science-la.summary_technical: JUSL: underground laboratory at 555 m depth at Jaduguda (East Singhbhum, Jharkhand); hosts the InDEx superheated-emulsion dark matter search. Operator, founding date and rock overburden in m.w.e. are not given in the sources read.

facility:jefferson-lab.summary_technical: DOE Office of Science national laboratory (Newport News, Virginia) operating CEBAF, a superconducting recirculating electron linac originally at 6 GeV and upgraded to 12 GeV (dedicated 2018); managed by SURATech, LLC.

notes: Several member states have suspended participation or the collaboration with Russian institutes is suspended in some projects (e.g. FAIR, PANDA); not modelled.
Only the NICA complex and its experiments are in this stream; JINR's other laboratories and external projects (NA61/SHINE, STAR, AMBER participation) are not recorded as JINR experiments.
facility:jinr-dubna.summary_technical: JINR: intergovernmental organisation founded by eleven states on 26 March 1956; the VBLHEP accelerator complex comprises the Nuclotron (1993), the Booster and the NICA collider (Run 1 from 25 March 2025) serving the BM@N fixed-target experiment, the MPD detector and the planned SPD.

notes: Facility record for the host institute of the Mainz neutrino-mass experiment; the university itself is institution:johannes-gutenberg-university-mainz.
facility:johannes-gutenberg-university-m.summary_technical: Institut für Physik, Johannes Gutenberg-Universität Mainz: host of the Mainz tritium beta-decay neutrino-mass experiment (MAC-E filter, phases I-III) that preceded KATRIN.

notes: This facility (the excavated underground laboratory beneath Dashi Hill, Kaiping, Jiangmen) is distinct from IHEP itself, which is the operating national laboratory; IHEP is recorded only as the operator, not as a separate facility record.
facility:juno-jiangmen.summary_technical: Underground laboratory beneath Dashi Hill, Kaiping, Jiangmen, Guangdong, China, with roughly 700 m of granite overburden, purpose-built to host the JUNO liquid-scintillator reactor-antineutrino detector 52.5 km from the Yangjiang and Taishan nuclear power plants.

notes: Plant described in the DANSS detector paper: "Kalinin Nuclear Power Plant (KNPP) located between Moscow and Saint Petersburg and exploiting four pressurized water reactors WWER-1000".
facility:kalinin-npp.summary_technical: Kalinin Nuclear Power Plant (KNPP), Udomlya, Tver Oblast, Russia: four VVER-1000 pressurised-water reactors (units 1-2 of project B-338, units 3-4 of project B-320), 3.1 GW thermal power per unit; host of the DANSS antineutrino spectrometer.

notes: The observatory also hosts KAGRA, CANDLES, NEWAGE and XENONnT R&D according to the ICRR facility page; only the Super-Kamiokande and Hyper-Kamiokande sites are recorded here.

The 1995 founding date is when ICRR's own page says the 'Kamioka Observatory' as a named administrative facility was established; it is not the date underground physics began at this site. The Mozumi mine location was already in scientific use well before 1995: Kamiokande (experiment:kamiokande) started taking data there in 1983, and Super-Kamiokande's cavity excavation (experiment:super-kamiokande, detector:super-kamiokande) began in December 1991. Both experiments therefore start before the observatory's formal 1995 establishment; this reflects the mine's long history of use against the administrative facility's later formal founding, and is not an error in the sourced dates.
facility:kamioka-observatory.summary_technical: Underground laboratory of the Institute for Cosmic Ray Research, University of Tokyo, in the Kamioka mine at Hida, Gifu. About 1000 m of rock (2700 m.w.e.) above Super-Kamiokande in the Mozumi mine; the Hyper-Kamiokande cavern is being built about 8 km south in the Tochibora mine.

notes: KEK's primary site is site:kek-tsukuba-belle-ii (the collider's Tsukuba hall), which has a sourced coordinate. site:kek-ps-k2k-beamline is a separate campus-grade point (approximate) for the 12 GeV proton synchrotron and the K2K beamline.
facility:kek.summary_technical: Inter-University Research Institute Corporation High Energy Accelerator Research Organization, Tsukuba, Ibaraki. Founded 1971 as the National Laboratory for High Energy Physics; reorganised in 1997. Host of the 12 GeV proton synchrotron (KEK-PS) that drove K2K, and co-operator of J-PARC.

notes: Facility record at the level needed for ECHo; the 163Ho is produced at ILL Grenoble and ion-implanted at the RISIKO facility in Mainz, neither recorded as a site here.
facility:kirchhoff-institute-for-physics.summary_technical: Kirchhoff-Institut für Physik (KIP), Heidelberg University: coordinates ECHo, fabricates the metallic magnetic calorimeter arrays in its cleanroom.

notes: Campus North is the site of the former Forschungszentrum Karlsruhe (founded 1956 as the Kernreaktor Bau- und Betriebsgesellschaft, later Kernforschungszentrum Karlsruhe); KIT as a legal entity dates from the merger with Universität Karlsruhe on 1 October 2009. The first interval is therefore the predecessor institution's, so that KASCADE (from 1996) and KASCADE-Grande (from 2003), which stood on the Forschungszentrum site before KIT existed, do not predate their host. No source read dates the Tritium Laboratory Karlsruhe itself.
This record covers KIT Campus North (the Tritium Laboratory Karlsruhe site) at the level needed for KATRIN's host-facility role; it is not a full record of KIT as a university/research organisation.
facility:kit-karlsruhe.summary_technical: KIT Campus North (Eggenstein-Leopoldshafen, Germany) hosts the Tritium Laboratory Karlsruhe, the site of the KATRIN experiment.

notes: Only the observatory facts needed for the DESI host record are recorded; other KPNO telescopes and tenant observatories are not.
facility:kitt-peak-national-observatory.summary_technical: NSF NOIRLab observatory on Kitt Peak, Arizona, at about 2100 m, founded 1958. Operates the 4-m Nicholas U. Mayall telescope on behalf of the DESI survey.

notes: Facility modelled as a single facility:km3net with two detector sites (ARCA off Capo Passero, Sicily and ORCA off Toulon, France), following the KM3NeT Letter of Intent's own framing of 'a network of deep-sea neutrino telescopes'. A third site, KM3NeT-Gr (Pylos, Greece), was named in the 2016 Letter of Intent as a candidate third building-block location but is not built and is not recorded here (no sourced detector or site record); the official 'ARCA and ORCA detectors' page (2026) describes only two operating sites.
No single legal operator has an institution record in the Atlas; the operator is given as free text only.
facility:km3net.summary_technical: Deep-sea Cherenkov neutrino observatory comprising two detector arrays under construction on the Mediterranean seabed: KM3NeT/ARCA (Capo Passero, Italy, ~3500 m depth) for high-energy astrophysical neutrinos and KM3NeT/ARCA neutrino astronomy, and KM3NeT/ORCA (Toulon, France, ~2450 m depth) for atmospheric neutrino oscillations and the neutrino mass ordering. Operated by the KM3NeT Collaboration; installation began December 2015 and continues with successive sea campaigns adding detection units to both sites.

notes: Operator not stated in any fetched source (the experiments were run by the Tata Institute of Fundamental Research with Osaka City University); left null.
facility:kolar-gold-fields-underground-l.summary_technical: Underground laboratory in the Kolar Gold Fields mines (Karnataka, India), at levels down to about 2.3 km of rock: cosmic-ray muon depth-intensity measurements, the 1965 atmospheric-neutrino telescopes, and the Phase I/II proton-decay detectors; ended with the mine closures from 1993.

notes: Kind `reactor_site` (as for Daya Bay and Chooz): the laboratory is inside the reactor building at a nuclear power station, 28 m from the core; it is also a shallow underground laboratory (~30 m.w.e.), but the reactor is what defines it.
The neutrino-physics programme of TEXONO (neutrino-electron scattering, magnetic moment, CEvNS searches) shares this facility; the dark-matter stream records only the germanium dark-matter work.
facility:kuo-sheng-reactor-neutrino-labo.summary_technical: Laboratory on the ground floor of the reactor building of the Kuo-Sheng Nuclear Power Station (2.9 GW thermal; Taiwan Power Company), 28 m from core #1, ~12 m below sea level with ~30 m.w.e. overburden; 4-pi passive shielding (5 cm Cu, 25 cm boron-loaded polyethylene, 5 cm steel, 15 cm Pb) plus cosmic-ray veto panels. First physics data July 2001. The power station was decommissioned in March 2023.

notes: This record covers the laboratory only as the host of the Bevatron and the antiproton experiment; other Berkeley Lab experiments belong to other streams.

Berkeley Lab History says the lab's legacy began in summer 1928, that the building later called the Rad Lab was committed to Lawrence on 26 August 1931, and that the University established the Radiation Laboratory as an independent entity on 1 July 1936; the founding interval uses 1931 at year precision.
institution:lawrence-berkeley-national-laboratory exists with facility_id null; linking it to this facility is left to the integrator (the record is another stream's).
facility:lawrence-berkeley-national-labo.summary_technical: Managed by the University of California for the DOE; successor of the Radiation Laboratory founded around the cyclotron in 1931. Operated the 6.5 GeV Bevatron proton synchrotron (1954-1993), on which Chamberlain, Segrè, Wiegand and Ypsilantis observed antiprotons in 1955.

notes: Host facility of CONUS+ since 2023 (the CONUS experiment's setup, relocated from facility:brokdorf-nuclear-power-plant).

Reactor thermal power (3.6 GWth) is from arXiv:2407.11912 and agrees with the 3,600 MW thermal power on the plant operator's reactor page (src:dw-kkl-reaktorgebaeude-und-reaktor), which also gives the General Electric BWR-6 type; the 1285 MW gross (1233 MW net) electrical rating is on src:dw-kkl-unser-kraftwerk. All are stated in the technical summary and not as separate numeric specs.
facility:leibstadt-nuclear-power-plant.summary_technical: Leibstadt Nuclear Power Plant (KKL), canton of Aargau, Switzerland; 3.6 GWth General Electric BWR-6 boiling water reactor (1285 MWe gross, 1233 MWe net rated); hosts CONUS+ (the relocated CONUS experiment) 20.7 m from the reactor core since 2023.

notes: The IHEP LHAASO site's inner pages (Observatory/Site, Scientific Goals) render as empty shells when fetched (JavaScript-driven content is not captured); construction and completion dates come from collaboration arXiv papers instead.
facility:lhaaso-daocheng.summary_technical: Multi-component high-altitude air-shower facility on Haizi Mountain, Daocheng County, Sichuan, China, at 4410 m altitude; operated by IHEP/Chinese Academy of Sciences.

notes: This record describes LNGS at a basic level (the laboratory and its Hall B, where ICARUS ran), not the full LNGS programme.

An m.w.e. overburden is not recorded as a spec here: the LNGS pages fetched give only the 1400 m rock thickness. L. Pandola's overview (arXiv:1102.0208) gives about 3100 m w.e. (minimum depth) and 3800 m w.e. (average depth), and the Borexino collaboration places Borexino at 3800 m w.e.

The foundation date of LNGS was not found on an official page; the excavation of the halls (1982-1987) is sourced to L. Pandola's overview (arXiv:1102.0208) and the laboratory's Italian description page, and the operating interval's start (1987) is the end of that excavation, marked uncertain.
facility:lngs.summary_technical: INFN national laboratory at Assergi (L'Aquila), Italy, with three underground halls of roughly 100 × 20 × 18 m under about 1400 m of rock, hosting low-background neutrino, dark matter and double-beta-decay experiments; the ICARUS T600 ran in Hall B from 2010 to 2013.

notes: The neutrino-oscillations topic is attached because LANSCE (as LAMPF) produced the neutrino beam for the LSND experiment.
facility:los-alamos-national-laboratory.summary_technical: DOE/NNSA national laboratory (Los Alamos, New Mexico), managed by Triad National Security, LLC; operates the LANSCE proton linac (Technical Area 53), historically LAMPF, whose beam-stop neutrinos fed the LSND experiment.

notes: Military origin (official history page, lsbb.eu/histoire): the strategic missile system of the Plateau d'Albion was in permanent operation from August 1971 to September 1996 and was dismantled in 1996; the LSBB comes from the reconversion of one of the two fire-control posts. The conversion date is not given in any source read.

Name: 'Laboratoire Souterrain à Bas Bruit' is the name on the laboratory's own website; the 1999 paper writes 'Laboratoire Souterrain à Bas Bruit de Rustrel-Pays d'Apt', and later papers translate it as Low Noise Underground Laboratory. Depth and overburden are on the site record.
The unit's supervisory bodies changed over time: SIMPLE papers of 2014 give 'UMS 3538 UNS/UAPV/CNRS'; the official site now gives 'UAR 3538' with CNRS and Avignon Université.
facility:lsbb-rustrel.summary_technical: Laboratoire Souterrain à Bas Bruit (LSBB), a CNRS / Avignon Université research support unit (UAR 3538) at Rustrel (Vaucluse), converted from one of the two former fire-control posts of the French strategic missile system on the Plateau d'Albion. The deepest experimental hall lies under 500 m of calcite rock (about 1500 m.w.e.) and holds a 100 m^2 floor on shock absorbers inside a steel Faraday cage; the GESA cavern used by SIMPLE is at 505 m depth.

notes: The facility record is the institute (a university laboratory), not the accelerators; its kind accelerator_laboratory follows the BNL/Jefferson Lab records.
facility:mainz-mami.summary_technical: Institut für Kernphysik, JGU Mainz (more than 150 employees): MAMI (racetrack and harmonic double-sided microtrons, 855 MeV and 1.5 GeV) with the A1 spectrometer and A2 Crystal Ball/TAPS halls; MESA energy-recovering superconducting linac (up to 155 MeV, 10 mA) under construction with P2, MAGIX and DarkMESA, within the PRISMA+ cluster of excellence.

notes: This is the NASA long-duration-balloon launch facility used to fly ANITA, not a detector site: ANITA takes data at float altitude (~37 km) over the Antarctic ice sheet, not at the launch point. Different ANITA flights launched from slightly different pads near McMurdo Station (LDB Camp for ANITA-LITE and ANITA-I; Williams Field for ANITA-II per the collaboration's own campaign pages); both are modelled as one facility here since no source distinguishes them as administratively separate.
facility:mcmurdo-ldb.summary_technical: NASA Columbia Scientific Balloon Facility (CSBF) long-duration-balloon launch operations near McMurdo Station, Antarctica, used to launch ANITA-LITE (2003), ANITA-I (2006), ANITA-II (2008, from Williams Field), ANITA-III (2014) and ANITA-IV (2016).

notes: This record describes MIT in its role as a physics-experiment host; the university itself is recorded separately as institution:massachusetts-institute-of-technology.
facility:mit.summary_technical: MIT Laboratory for Nuclear Science / Department of Physics (Cambridge, MA), host institution of the Winslow group's ABRACADABRA-10 cm and successor lumped-element axion dark-matter searches.

facility:modane-underground-laboratory.summary_technical: CNRS/IN2P3 underground laboratory located mid-way through the Frejus road tunnel near Modane, Savoie, France, under ~1700 m of rock; founded 1981; since 2019 a national platform attached to LPSC Grenoble.

notes: Other experiments are known to have used the laboratory (for example the Liquid Scintillation Detector, running from October 1984 according to a 1985 ICRC paper found in a search) but were not researched here; the record is the minimal facility NUSEX needs.
Status 'active' reflects only the open interval; whether the laboratory still operates was not established.
facility:mont-blanc-laboratory.summary_technical: Cave laboratory half way along the Mont Blanc road tunnel at about 5000 m.w.e.; host of NUSEX (1982-) and later experiments. Founding date, operator and later history not established.

notes: The cyclotron is not an Atlas accelerator record (not assigned to this stream); the experiment records it in a note. The facility's founding date was not found: the first dated use of the machine in the sources is Lederman's 1950 pion-beam work.
facility:nevis-laboratories.summary_technical: Columbia Physics Department's Nevis Laboratories, Irvington-on-Hudson, New York; hosted a 400 MeV synchrocyclotron (external pion and muon beams from about 1950).

notes: Created by the precision-2 stream as the host of the NIST beam neutron-lifetime experiments.
facility:nist-center-for-neutron-researc.summary_technical: NIST Center for Neutron Research: national user facility built around the NBSR research reactor (first critical 7 December 1967), with thermal and cold neutron beams. In this Atlas it hosts the beam neutron-lifetime experiments BL1, BL2 and BL3. Shut down 3 February 2021; reactor operations resumed in May 2026.

notes: kind is recorded as `research_laboratory` (the facility kinds have no better fit for a large multiprogram DOE laboratory); the SNS accelerator itself is a separate record, accelerator:sns.

The facility's marker is the Spallation Neutron Source complex (site:ornl-sns-complex), the only ORNL site in the Atlas; it is not ORNL's main entrance, and the laboratory's other campuses are not mapped.
facility:oak-ridge-national-laboratory.summary_technical: DOE Office of Science multiprogram national laboratory (Oak Ridge, Tennessee), managed by UT-Battelle, LLC; operates the Spallation Neutron Source (SNS) and High Flux Isotope Reactor among other user facilities.

notes: No operator is recorded: the GRAPES-3 papers list "The GRAPES-3 Experiment, Cosmic Ray Laboratory, Raj Bhavan, Ooty 643001, India" and the Tata Institute of Fundamental Research as affiliations but do not say who operates the laboratory.
The GRAPES-3 collaboration website (grapes-3.tifr.res.in) could not be reached (DNS failure and timeouts, checked 2026-10-26).
facility:ooty-cosmic-ray-laboratory.summary_technical: Cosmic Ray Laboratory, Raj Bhavan, Ooty 643001, the address the GRAPES-3 papers give for the experiment (authors are also affiliated with the Tata Institute of Fundamental Research, Mumbai); altitude 2200 m.

notes: Located in the Tentsuji Tunnel (5 km) between Oto village and Nishiyoshino village in Nara prefecture, about 100 km south of Osaka (RCNP annual report).
Created by the nai-rest stream for ELEGANT V and the early PICO-LON measurements; no website of the observatory was found (the RCNP group page is the closest official description).
facility:oto-cosmo-observatory.summary_technical: RCNP (Osaka University) Oto Cosmo Observatory in the centre of the 5 km Tentsuji Tunnel between Oto village and Nishiyoshino village, Nara; maximum overburden about 500 m (1400 m.w.e.), cosmic-ray flux 1e-7 cm^-2 s^-1, radon about 10 Bq/m3; experimental rooms 3 km from the Oto entrance.

notes: Reactor power: "The plant consists of three identical pressurized water reactors with a total thermal power of 11.63 GW" (PRD 64, 112001).
facility:palo-verde-ngs.summary_technical: Palo Verde Nuclear Generating Station, Maricopa County, Arizona: three identical pressurised-water reactors with a total thermal power of 11.63 GW; host of the Palo Verde reactor-antineutrino oscillation experiment (750 m and 890 m baselines).

notes: No website for the park itself is recorded: no park site was fetched. CONICYT's astronomy news page is cited for the opening and the concession.

Sourced site names differ by experiment (ACT: "slopes of Cerro Toco"; POLARBEAR: "James Ax Observatory ... on Cerro Toco"; CLASS: "Cerro Toco"; Simons Observatory: "near the summit of Cerro Toco"); all four are on Cerro Toco within about a kilometre of each other and all four papers/pages place them in the Parque Astronómico Atacama. See the four site records.

SWGO (proposed) is hosted here at Pampa La Bola; its site record carries only a regional-anchor coordinate because no source gives Pampa La Bola's longitude. The park's concession page names "the area called Pampa La Bola, Llano de Chajnantor".
facility:parque-astronomico-atacama.summary_technical: Astronomical park of about 36,000 ha on the Llano de Chajnantor (San Pedro de Atacama, Antofagasta Region), held by CONICYT under a 50-year territorial concession from January 2014. Hosts ground-based CMB experiments at ~5200 m on Cerro Toco: ACT (2007-2022), POLARBEAR/Simons Array, CLASS and the Simons Observatory; the baseline Chilean site of the proposed CMB-S4 (cancelled 2025). Also the chosen host site (Pampa La Bola, 4770 m) of the proposed SWGO gamma-ray observatory, selected August 2024.

notes: operator/operator_text left null: no fetched source names a distinct legal operator; the Observatory is run by the international Pierre Auger Collaboration itself.
facility:pierre-auger-observatory.summary_technical: Hybrid ultra-high-energy cosmic-ray observatory in Mendoza Province, Argentina, combining a 3000 km² surface array of 1660 water-Cherenkov detector stations with 27 fluorescence telescopes in four buildings overlooking the array; operated by the international Pierre Auger Collaboration since inauguration in November 2008, currently undergoing the AugerPrime upgrade.

notes: 2026-09-17 re-check: psi.ch is reachable (homepage, /en/about, /en/about/history-of-psi, /en/cas/hipa, and the HIPA-turns-50 news story all returned content); earlier 404s on every attempted psi.ch URL do not reproduce. Founding date, website and the ETH-Domain membership line are sourced to PSI and ETH Board pages.
facility:psi.summary_technical: Swiss multidisciplinary research institute (Villigen/Wurenlingen, Aargau), part of the ETH Domain; formed in 1988 from the merger of EIR and SIN; operates the HIPA ring cyclotron feeding muon and spallation-neutron sources used by MEG/MEG-II and (planned) Mu3e.

notes: This facility is shared: experiment:ctao and experiment:magic both list it in their facility roles.

The observatory's start is the 1985 official inauguration (IAC history page), earlier than HEGRA (1987) and MAGIC (2003); the second interval records when MAGIC-I began gamma-ray work here, not the observatory's founding. Status 'active' reflects that the hosted experiments are operating (checked 2026-09-17).
facility:roque-de-los-muchachos-observat.summary_technical: Astronomical observatory on the island of La Palma, Canary Islands, Spain, hosting the MAGIC telescopes and CTAO-North (the northern array of the Cherenkov Telescope Array Observatory).

notes: Reactor-neutrino physics happened here only as a guest experiment: the site is a DOE production and cleanup site, not a physics laboratory.

The official SRS timeline lists "Neutrino confirmed at P Reactor" under 1956 and "R Reactor startup" under an earlier year heading whose digits were lost in the page text; the active interval therefore starts with the 1954 P, L, K reactor startups and is marked approximate.
facility:savannah-river-site.summary_technical: Savannah River Site (formerly Savannah River Plant): 310 square miles in Aiken, Barnwell and Allendale counties, South Carolina; five production reactors built from 1951 (R, P, K, L, C). Host of the Cowan–Reines reactor-antineutrino experiment at P Reactor, 1955-1956.

facility:sck-cen-mol.summary_technical: SCK CEN (Belgian Nuclear Research Centre), Mol, Belgium: BR2 is an open-pool research reactor burning highly enriched uranium (93.5 % 235U) at 40-100 MW_th with a compact (about 50 cm x 80 cm) core; host of the SoLid antineutrino detector at 6.3-8.9 m.

notes: The official hawc-observatory.org site could not be fetched (TLS certificate verification failed on every attempt, checked 2026-09-17); all facts come from collaboration arXiv papers instead.
facility:sierra-negra.summary_technical: High-altitude gamma-ray observatory site on Sierra Negra, Puebla, Mexico, at 4100 m altitude; hosts the HAWC water-Cherenkov array, operating since March 2015.

notes: 2026-09-17 re-check: www6.slac.stanford.edu is reachable (an earlier TLS-certificate error on slac.stanford.edu does not reproduce there). Website and operator are upgraded to this official source. The founding year (1962) is taken from SLAC's own "At a glance" page, which gives the year but no day.
facility:slac.summary_technical: DOE Office of Science national laboratory (Menlo Park, California), operated by Stanford University; historically home to the 3.2 km SLAC linac (up to 50 GeV electrons), the SLC electron-positron collider (1989-1998) and the PEP-II B-factory (1999-2008).

notes: Facility status is `active` because no source consulted says the SM-3 reactor itself has stopped; the interval only covers the Neutrino-4 use.
facility:sm-3-reactor-dimitrovgrad.summary_technical: SM-3 research reactor of the State Science Center Research Institute of Atomic Reactors (RIAR), Dimitrovgrad, Russia: compact 42 x 42 x 35 cm^3 core, highly enriched 235U, 90 MW thermal power; host of the Neutrino-4 experiment.

notes: No official page consulted gives a numeric m.w.e. (metres water equivalent) shielding figure or a founding year distinct from the SNO legacy; both are left unrecorded rather than guessed. The commonly quoted '6010 m.w.e.' figure could not be re-confirmed on an official page and is therefore NOT recorded.

The operating-start date (March 2011) is the date SNOLAB's own April 2011 update page gives for the last area of the laboratory being opened, so that the entire lab operates as a clean lab (archived copy); it marks the full expanded laboratory, not the earlier SNO cavern, and is marked approximate.
facility:snolab.summary_technical: Class-2000 clean-room underground laboratory at the 6800 ft level (~2070 m rock overburden) of Vale's Creighton nickel mine near Sudbury, Ontario, reached via 9 Shaft; an expansion of the original SNO cavern, governed by a consortium of five Canadian universities.

notes: CDMS II is mentioned here only in this note: the Soudan page states "The MINOS neutrino experiment and the CDMS2 dark matter search are the two largest projects". CDMS II has its own record, experiment:cdms-ii.
No official closure date for the laboratory was found in the sources consulted; the decommissioning interval is marked uncertain.
facility:soudan-underground-laboratory.summary_technical: University of Minnesota underground facility in the Soudan iron mine at 705 m depth (2070 m.w.e.), host of the 5.4 kt MINOS far detector (2003-2016) and, on the same level, the CDMS II cryogenic dark matter experiment.

notes: The CDMS papers place the facility 'in the Hansen Experimental Physics Laboratory, on the Stanford University campus', not at SLAC; SLAC's Menlo Park site (site:slac-menlo-park-campus) is a different location, so a separate facility is recorded.
No operator is stated in the CDMS papers; operator_text is left null rather than inferred.

Overburden: the CDMS papers give ~16 m.w.e. (arXiv:astro-ph/0203500, astro-ph/0002471) and ~17 m.w.e. (arXiv:astro-ph/9712343, astro-ph/0405033, 1010.4290); 17 is recorded (three sources, latest paper).
facility:stanford-underground-facility.summary_technical: Shallow underground facility (10.6 m below ground level, ~17 m.w.e.) in the Hansen Experimental Physics Laboratory on the Stanford campus; housed the CDMS I Ge/Si bolometers and the first tower of CDMS II ZIP detectors behind a 15 cm lead / 25 cm polyethylene shield with a scintillator muon veto. Separate from SLAC (Menlo Park).

notes: Depth and overburden are on the site record. The laboratory's own page gives no depth figure; the depth comes from the SABRE South papers.
facility:stawell-underground-physics-lab.summary_technical: Underground laboratory at 1024 m depth (about 2900 m water equivalent) in the Stawell Gold Mine, western Victoria, reached by a decline (helical access road); 260 m^2 of precision laboratory space, about half occupied by SABRE South. Operated by SUPL Ltd; construction completed and laboratory unveiled August 2022.

notes: A project-level facility: the proposed STCF is not built; there is no operating laboratory yet. It exists so that the proposed collider, its experiment and its area marker have a host; its lead institution is the University of Science and Technology of China (USTC).
facility:stcf-hefei.summary_technical: STCF project site in Hefei, Anhui: Future Big Science City, about 1 km², three candidate sites under geological exploration; Anhui, Hefei and USTC fund the key-technology R&D (364 M CNY) from 2023; construction proposed for the 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-2030).

facility:summit-station-greenland.summary_technical: Summit Station: year-round research station at the summit of the Greenland ice sheet, 72°N 38°W, elevation 3200 m, operated by Battelle Arctic Research Operations for the NSF Arctic Research Program; hosts the Radio Neutrino Observatory Greenland (RNO-G).

facility:surf.summary_technical: Underground laboratory operated by the South Dakota Science and Technology Authority in the former Homestake mine. The 4850-foot level (4850 ft = 1478 m below the surface, rounded to 1500 m in some sources; 4300 m.w.e.) hosts LZ, the Majorana Demonstrator, CASPAR and the LBNF/DUNE far-detector campus.

notes: Plant description from the TAO CDR: "Taishan Nuclear Power Plant locates in Chixi town of Taishan city in Guangdong province, 53 km from the JUNO experiment. It has two cores currently in operation."
facility:taishan-npp.summary_technical: Taishan Nuclear Power Plant, Chixi town, Taishan city, Guangdong, 53 km from JUNO: two EPR cores of 4.6 GW thermal power each in operation (two more possibly later); host of the JUNO-TAO near detector.

notes: telescopearray.org and its known mirrors could not be reached (DNS failures, connection refused, or 502 errors on every attempt, checked 2026-09-17); all quantitative facts here come from a 2026 collaboration arXiv paper instead of the official site.
operator/operator_text left null: no fetched source names a distinct legal operator; the observatory is run by the international Telescope Array Collaboration.
facility:telescope-array-utah.summary_technical: Hybrid ultra-high-energy cosmic-ray observatory near Delta, Utah, USA, at about 1400 m altitude, comprising a 507-counter surface-detector array over ~700 km² and three fluorescence-detector stations; operating since 11 May 2008 and extended since 2019 by the four-times-larger TAx4 array.

notes: The facility has no operator and no national jurisdiction in the sources read (country list left empty): the paper gives only the geographic position and the ocean region. Its place is also recorded on the site.
facility:trident-south-china-sea-site.summary_technical: Abyssal plain at a depth of ~3.5 km in the north-eastern South China Sea near 114.0 E, 17.4 N: sea current speed < 10 cm/s below 3 km, absorption length ~27 m and scattering length ~63 m for Cherenkov light (T-REX pathfinder measurements).

notes: Created by the precision-2 stream as the host of PiENu (pion decay) and TUCAN (ultracold-neutron EDM).
facility:triumf.summary_technical: TRIUMF (Vancouver, BC), Canada’s particle accelerator centre, established 1968 and owned by a consortium of 21 Canadian universities. In this Atlas it hosts the PiENu and TUCAN precision experiments.

notes: No operator is recorded: the TAIGA lecture names Leonid Kuzmichev as the head of the Tunka facility but no operating institution.
The TAIGA website (taiga-experiment.info) returned HTTP 404 and the other candidate hosts did not resolve (checked 2026-10-26).
facility:tunka-valley.summary_technical: Tunka astrophysical facility, 50 km west of the southern tip of Lake Baikal; since 1993 it grew from Tunka-4 (four phototubes) through Tunka-25 and Tunka-133 to the TAIGA complex (2012 onward).

notes: Facility record at the level needed for HOLMES; detectors are also made and tested at NIST (Boulder) and the 163Ho is produced at ILL Grenoble, none of which is recorded as a site here.
facility:university-of-milano-bicocca.summary_technical: University of Milano-Bicocca (with INFN Sezione di Milano-Bicocca) laboratory hosting the HOLMES 163Ho TES-microcalorimeter programme; the ERC grant's host institution is INFN.

notes: No founding or establishment date for CENPA itself is sourced; only its current hosting of ADMX is sourced (checked 2026-09-17).

The commonly cited history that ADMX was built at Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory in 1995 and moved to CENPA in 2010 has no checkable primary citation; it is NOT recorded as a dated interval here. A primary source for these dates is still needed.
facility:university-of-washington-cenpa.summary_technical: University of Washington research laboratory (North Physics Lab building, 4311 Mason Place NE, Seattle) hosting nuclear/astro-particle experiments including the Gen 2 Axion Dark Matter eXperiment (ADMX), which moved to CENPA from Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory.

notes: The facility was named the Large Synoptic Survey Telescope (LSST) before December 2019; the Rubin history page dates the Congressional act confirming the new name to December 2019.
facility:vera-c-rubin-observatory.summary_technical: NSF–DOE observatory on Cerro Pachón, Chile, operated by NSF NOIRLab and SLAC; houses the 8.4-m Simonyi Survey Telescope and LSST Camera for the 10-year Legacy Survey of Space and Time.

notes: Created for DELight, which names this laboratory as its phase-I host (arXiv:2512.15278); no Atlas facility existed for it. The only Atlas experiment placed here.
No official laboratory website was found; operator not stated in the sources read (the DELight paper says GeMSE is 'operated by collaboration members').
facility:vue-des-alpes-underground-labor.summary_technical: Small underground space in the Vue-des-Alpes tunnel (canton of Neuchâtel, Switzerland) with 235 m of rock overburden (620 m.w.e.), electricity and network access only; hosts the GeMSE low-background HPGe screening facility (described by Freiburg- and Bern-based authors; the DELight TAUP 2025 paper says it is operated by DELight collaboration members); named as the phase-I site of DELight (TAUP 2025).

notes: WIPP is primarily a U.S. Department of Energy transuranic nuclear-waste repository; it hosted the EXO-200 double-beta-decay experiment as a secondary underground physics use. The official DOE page gives the facility's opening year (1999); see the interval's note.
facility:wipp.summary_technical: DOE transuranic-waste geologic repository in a salt bed near Carlsbad, New Mexico, with storage rooms ~2150 ft (655 m) underground; hosted the EXO-200 136Xe double-beta-decay detector from 2011 to 2018.

notes: No operator is recorded: the sources describe a Japanese-Australian collaboration (University of Adelaide and Japanese universities, arXiv:2406.15037) but name no legal operator of the site.
No live website: the collaboration home page survives only on the Internet Archive (the icrhp9.icrr.u-tokyo.ac.jp host no longer resolves).
facility:woomera-cangaroo-site.summary_technical: Observing site of the CANGAROO imaging atmospheric Cherenkov telescopes near Woomera, South Australia, 160 m a.s.l.: the 3.8 m telescope (CANGAROO-I), the 7 m / 10 m CANGAROO-II telescope and the four-telescope 10 m CANGAROO-III array. Observations stopped in 2011.

notes: The facility and the experiment coincide (the array is the facility); the experiment record is experiment:yakutsk-eas-array.
facility:yakutsk-eas-array.summary_technical: Yakutsk EAS array: scintillation, underground-muon and air-Cherenkov detectors on a triangular grid near Oktyomtsy, operating since the 1970s, last modernised 2019-2021, studying cosmic rays above about 1 PeV.

notes: No founding date for Wright Laboratory itself is sourced.
facility:yale-wright-lab.summary_technical: Yale University's nuclear/particle/astrophysics research building at 272 Whitney Avenue, New Haven, CT, host site of the HAYSTAC axion haloscope and other precision experiments.

notes: The facility name follows the abstract of the ARGO-YBJ detector paper ("YangBaJing Cosmic Ray Observatory"); the experiments also call it the Yangbajing Laboratory or Yangbajing High Altitude Cosmic Ray Laboratory.
No operator is recorded: the sources describe collaborations (ICRR and Chinese institutes; INFN and CAS) rather than a single operating body.
facility:yangbajing-cosmic-ray-observato.summary_technical: Yangbajing laboratory, 90 km north of Lhasa at 4300 m (606 g/cm2): home of the Tibet AS-gamma array (Tibet-I from 1990, Tibet-III from 1999) and ARGO-YBJ (2006-2013).

notes: primary_site_id points at site:y2l-yangyang, one point for the whole laboratory (A5 and A6 are separate tunnels; the COSINE-100 muon-detector paper, arXiv:1712.02011, puts the KIMS site about 200 m from the COSINE site).

Depth in m.w.e. differs between papers (about 1800, 2000 and 2400 m.w.e. are all quoted); see the site record's note. The overburden (700 m) is consistent across papers, but one 2023 IBS slide deck says 600 m.
facility:yangyang-underground-laboratory.summary_technical: Y2L: experimental areas in the A5 and A6 work tunnels next to the underground generators of the Yangyang pumped-storage plant, reached by a 2 km horizontal access tunnel; minimum granite overburden 700 m (muon flux 3.8e-7 /cm2/s in A5, 2.7e-7 /cm2/s in A6). A6 (~100 m2) was completed in 2003 for the KIMS CsI(Tl) experiment; A5 (~200 m2) was added by the IBS Center for Underground Physics in 2013-14 for AMoRE and COSINE. Equipment was being relocated to Yemilab from 2023.

notes: Yemilab was also proposed as host of non-dark-matter projects (large liquid-scintillator detector in the LSC pit, IsoDAR); those belong to the neutrino stream and are not recorded here.
Y2L slide deck of 2023: '2022.10.05 The construction completion ceremony' and '2023.08 - 2024.09 Y2L relocation to Yemilab'.
facility:yemilab.summary_technical: Yemilab: ~1,000 m overburden (about 2,500 m.w.e.) at the end of a 782 m access tunnel (12% slope) from the bottom of the Handuk mine's second shaft; limestone host rock; 17 experimental rooms including the AMoRE Hall (21 x 21 x 16 m, floor at 1,029 m depth) and the LSC Hall with a cylindrical pit of ~6,200 m3; preliminary muon flux 1.0e-7 /cm2/s, about four times lower than at Y2L. Construction September 2017 to September 2022; relocation from Y2L from 2023.

notes: RENO's own official site domains (reno.snu.ac.kr, home.kias.re.kr/MKG/h/reno) failed DNS/connection when tried; this record relies on the 2012 arXiv discovery paper, INSPIRE, and OpenStreetMap reactor-building footprints with the RENO design-report baselines (used for the approximate hall coordinates).
facility:yonggwang-hanbit-reactor-site.summary_technical: Reactor-neutrino site at the Hanbit (Yonggwang) Nuclear Power Plant, South Korea, hosting the RENO near (294 m) and far (1383 m) detector halls, 6 × 2.8 GW_th reactor array.

notes: This is the Experiment Hall building, not the storage-ring orbit. The Atomic Energy Commission chose a 6,800-acre site at Weston, Illinois, on 7 December 1966 (Fermilab History and Archives). The OpenStreetMap outline drawn here encloses about 6,817 acres (computed from its coordinates), so it is drawn from that date. It is the outline as mapped in 2026, not a survey of the boundary in earlier years.

The detector ran at Gran Sasso from 2010 to 2013 and was overhauled at CERN from 2014, so no Fermilab building stood for it in those years; the 2015 short-baseline proposal describes it as "a new building". The building is drawn from July 2017, when Fermilab News describes the detector arriving to be placed outside "the Short-Baseline Neutrino Far Detector building" until it is installed "inside the new ICARUS building"; the detector moved in on 14 August 2018 ("a recently completed building"). notes: The IceCube coordinate frame is anchored: the IceCube instrumentation paper (arXiv:1612.05093, version 3 of 6 Feb 2024, section 5.3) states that the y-axis is aligned with the Prime Meridian (Grid North, towards Greenwich) and the x-axis points 90 degrees clockwise (Grid East), and the IceCube repository i3astropy gives the nominal location of the detector centre (lat -89.9944, lon -62.6081, height 883.9 m, the elevation of the frame origin). Earlier versions of the paper may not state the orientation; docs.icecube.aq returned HTTP 401 to every fetch attempt (checked 2026-10-25).

Absolute accuracy of the IceCube features is about 500 m (anchor of unstated epoch, ice drift about 10 m a year, and the OpenStreetMap point for IceCube, 89.99 S 63.4531 W, lies 489 m away); the relative layout of strings and tanks is good to about 1 m and drawn at true size and orientation.

String and tank positions come from the IC86 geometry text file in the IceCube repository icecube/toise (strings) and the GraphNeT copy of the same geometry (IceTop tanks, checked against the IceTop paper).md.
String and tank groups are drawn as MultiPolygons of small markers because the map format has no multi-point type; each record is split to stay within 400 vertices.

Overpass (queried 2026-10-25, extract timestamp 2026-10-25T10:37:51Z) holds only the station village node, the ceremonial pole node and the IceCube office node near the pole; no IceCube Laboratory building or station building footprint is mapped.
map:amundsen-scott-south-pole-station.summary_technical: Local map for facility:amundsen-scott-south-pole-station. IceCube in-ice string positions (strings 1-86) are the mean horizontal positions of each string's DOMs in the IC86 geometry file published in the IceCube repository icecube/toise; IceTop tank positions come from the GraphNeT copy of the same geometry. The IceCube coordinate frame (y along the Prime Meridian, grid north; x grid east) is placed with its origin at the nominal detector location from icecube/i3astropy, in a South Pole azimuthal-equidistant plane. Relative layout about 1 m; absolute placement about 500 m. ARA stations, AMANDA, the IceCube Upgrade strings and IceCube-Gen2 remain unlocated.

map:argonne-national-laboratory.summary_technical: One local map for facility:argonne-national-laboratory. Drawn from OpenStreetMap: the campus fence polygon (way 4372309), the APS Experiment Hall multipolygon (relation 3126234), the APS linac tunnel (411) and injection wing (412) buildings, and Building 203 (the ATLAS building). Derived: the APS storage-ring orbit as a circle of the published 1103.609 m circumference, concentric with the hall's circular outlines (accuracy 10 m). Not drawn: the internal layout of ATLAS.

notes: Eleven clusters (88 strings) are drawn, one record each, with the year of deployment as the record's own validity start so the timeline shows the array growing (1: 2016 ... 11: 2023). Positions are read from the to-scale top view of arXiv:2309.16310 (ICRC 2023, Fig. 1 right panel) registered to the measured string positions of arXiv:2108.00212 (Fig. 2, X east, Y north): 63 of 64 dots within 8 m, rms 3.1 m. Relative layout about 5 m; neither source states the frame origin.

The absolute position of the whole pattern is only good to about 1500 m: the published site coordinate is rounded to a minute (1.85 km in latitude, 1.15 km in longitude) and does not say which part of the field it marks; the pattern's centroid is placed on it. The 2013 early-construction paper (arXiv:1308.1833) gives 51 50' N, 104 20' E, 8.7 km away; the 2020-2025 papers (arXiv:2011.09209, 2309.16310, 2412.00164, 2507.01893) all give 51 46' N, 104 24' E, which is used. Shore distance: "about 3.6 km offshore" (2023, 2024) versus "about 4 km from the shore" (2025).

Not drawn: clusters 12 and 13 (incomplete in the 2023 figure), clusters 14 to 16 (no top view; the telescope had 14 clusters, 117 strings and 4212 optical modules by April 2025 per arXiv:2507.01893, 16 clusters by 2026 per the JINR site), the inter-cluster and laser strings, and the shore station (no source gives a coordinate for it; arXiv:1308.1833 says only that the site is near the outfall of the Ivanovka river).

The previous single 60 m circle at the site point (geometry:baikal-gvd-cluster-footprint, a cluster placed at the coordinate by assumption) is removed: the clusters now carry their real arrangement. The site point (geometry:baikal-gvd-site-point) is kept as the anchor marker.

The cluster spacing is not a uniform lattice: the nearest-neighbour distance of a cluster centre runs from 201 m to 266 m on this layout (the papers say "approximately 300 m", reduced to 250 m in 2022); the figures were not forced onto a lattice.
map:baikal-deep-underwater-neutrino-tele.summary_technical: Local map for facility:baikal-deep-underwater-neutrino-telescope. Clusters 1-11 (8 strings each) are read from the top view of arXiv:2309.16310, registered to the measured positions of arXiv:2108.00212 (63 dots within 8 m, rms 3.1 m), and centred on the published 51 46' N, 104 24' E (accuracy 1500 m). Deployment years from the figure legend are each record's validity start. Clusters 12-16, inter-cluster strings and the shore station are not drawn.

notes: This map is thin: the surface administrative building, the Neutrino settlement and the Main adit entrance are drawn from OpenStreetMap, but the tunnel path and the SAGE underground hall are not, because no source consulted gives the tunnel's path or bearing and OpenStreetMap does not appear to trace it (no way was found by a Nominatim name search for 'Baksan tunnel' or Cyrillic equivalents).

SAGE's own 1999 paper (src:sage-1999-capture-rate) states the laboratory is '3.5 km from the entrance of a horizontal adit excavated into the side of Mount Andyrchi' with a 60x10x12 m chamber (src:geo-euro-ug-pandola-2011). Drawing it would need a topographic source, or an OpenStreetMap trace of the tunnel, giving the tunnel's bearing.
The Main adit entrance is drawn from an OpenStreetMap node. The unlocated row cites the official INR distances (550 m to BUST, 3.5 km to SAGE) and halls; the tunnel path and halls are not drawn.
map:baksan-neutrino-observatory.summary_technical: One local map for facility:baksan-neutrino-observatory. Only surface features (OSM: the BNO administrative building, way 1504181774; the Neutrino settlement, way 206835293; the Main adit entrance, node/4244310615) are drawn. site:baksan-sage-underground-lab is not drawn: SAGE's own 1999 paper gives its distance from the adit entrance (3.5 km) but not the tunnel's bearing, and no OpenStreetMap trace of the tunnel was found.

notes: This map is thin: it can draw the mine's surface works site (traced from aerial imagery) and a sourced depth for the underground level, but no source consulted locates the specific shaft or the underground laboratory workings within that surface footprint. No detector is placed at site:boulby-mine in the Atlas (ZEPLIN and DRIFT, which the laboratory has hosted, are not yet Atlas entities), so no entity besides the site itself needs accounting here.

The two primary shaft collars (OSM 'Man Shaft (Downcast)' and 'Rock Shaft (Upcast)') and two shaft-head buildings are drawn. The mine's surface boundary is an OSM landuse outline. The underground laboratory itself is not drawn.
map:boulby-underground-laboratory.summary_technical: OSM surface works outline, shaft collars and shaft-head buildings (georeferenced); 1.1 km shaft depth and 2840 m.w.e. from the AION workshop summary and DarkSPHERE paper; laboratory workings unlocated.

notes: The 'Reaktorgebaeude' polygon (way 87723028, 9227 m2, 130 m span) is the whole reactor-building complex, not the containment cylinder; its circular arc (radius 40.2 m) suggests the axis lies ~21 m SSW of the polygon centroid, but no source states the core position, so the CONUS point keeps the centroid with 40 m accuracy.
map:brokdorf-nuclear-power-plant.summary_technical: Reactor-building footprint from OpenStreetMap (georeferenced); CONUS drawn as a derived point at the building centroid with accuracy widened for the unresolved 17.1 m offset (arXiv:2401.07684). The interim fuel store outline is cross-checked against BASE's stated 93 m x 27 m (perimeter, 6 %); the turbine hall is context.

notes: All three of this facility's Atlas sites (site:bnl-upton-campus, site:bnl-rhic-ip6-star, site:bnl-rhic-ip8-phenix-sphenix) and both of its Atlas accelerators (accelerator:rhic, accelerator:ags) are drawn; nothing is listed as not drawn. Buildings 930 (Linear Accelerator), 901 (Tandem Van de Graaff) and 942 (AGS Booster) are drawn as context features not linked to an entity, because the Atlas has no accelerator records for the linac or the Booster.

The campus boundary (geometry:bnl-upton-campus-boundary) is OSM relation 18896697, fetched through the Nominatim search API; an Overpass query for a boundary polygon (comparable to CERN's Meyrin/Prévessin fence lines) could not be completed.

E949 (Brookhaven AGS experiment, K+ -> pi+ nu nu-bar) has no Atlas site or detector record of its own (its facility roles reference facility:brookhaven-national-laboratory only), so nothing about it is drawn or listed as not drawn; a candidate location (Building 912, 'AGS Exp. Area', drawn here as geometry:bnl-ags-experimental-area-building) would be the place to start if a site record is added.
map:brookhaven-national-laboratory.summary_technical: One local map for facility:brookhaven-national-laboratory spanning the RHIC and AGS ring footprints and the adjoining accelerator-complex buildings on the Upton campus. Geometry sourced from OpenStreetMap (way 50074088 for the RHIC ring, tagged tunnel=yes/indoor=yes; way 289305285 for the AGS ring, tagged place=locality) cross-checked against BNL's published RHIC circumference (2.4 mi) and the AGS's 1960 design-specification mean radius (421.5 ft), plus OSM building footprints for the STAR (1006/1006A) and PHENIX/sPHENIX (1008/1008A) halls corroborated against BNL's own central-campus-map building-number key.

notes: The site coordinate of site:lsc-canfranc used to be the same OSM feature as geometry:canfranc-surface-building (42.7493154, -0.5162702, precision_m 500), the laboratory's administrative offices at Canfranc-Estación, about 3.0 km from the underground laboratory itself (geometry:canfranc-lab-underground, an independently OSM-tagged feature 'Galería de evacuación 12', Aía); it has been replaced by the point of geometry:canfranc-lab-underground.

The historic Canfranc railway tunnel is only partially traced in OpenStreetMap (about 1.28 km of a tunnel usually cited at ~7.8 km); geometry:canfranc-tunnel-rail-somport-stub is drawn as a partial trace rather than extended by guesswork. A fuller OpenStreetMap trace or a surveyed tunnel plan would allow the whole tunnel to be drawn.
map:canfranc-underground-laboratory.summary_technical: One local map for facility:canfranc-underground-laboratory. The Somport road tunnel (OSM ways 29050143 + 76450688 + 1356486837, length-checked at 0.34% against a civil-engineering journal article) is drawn as context, alongside a partial trace of the historic rail tunnel. The laboratory itself is a separately OSM-tagged feature (way 1075274236) about 3.0 km from the surface administrative building at Canfranc-Estación (way 711426145).

notes: site:cern-lep-point-2-l3 and site:cern-point-2-alice, and site:cern-lep-point-8-delphi and site:cern-point-8-lhcb, are drawn as separate geometry features using the same underlying OSM polygon (the same physical Point 2 / Point 8 enclosure hosted a LEP experiment 1989-2000 and has hosted an LHC experiment since), so the two shapes in each pair are identical.

MapCERN's public Facilities layer (CERN GIS) names the SPS access buildings (868-873 = BA1-BA6), SR8 (2875), the HL-LHC buildings (SD/SE/SU/SF/SHM 17 and 57) and the ECN3 access and counting-room buildings (911, 918); the OpenStreetMap polygons carry those numbers, which is why name searches for UA1, UA2, CAST and ECN3 find nothing. UA1 and UA2 (underground in ECX5 and ECX4), CAST (SR8) and ECN3 (underground cavern, building 900) are therefore shown by the surface buildings that serve them, not by their own outlines; the HL-LHC surface buildings are drawn, its new shafts and galleries are not.
map:cern.summary_technical: One local map for facility:cern spanning the Meyrin and Prévessin sites and the full LHC/LEP tunnel footprint. Geometry sourced from OpenStreetMap (relation 9512017 for the LHC/LEP ring; ways 66473762/174646428/309914733 for SPS/PS/PSB; named Point-N surface enclosures for ATLAS/ALICE/CMS/LHCb and their LEP-era predecessors L3/ALEPH/DELPHI) cross-checked against CERN's published circumference and depth figures, plus one CMS-paper surveyed cavern point and two ring-derived points for FASER/SND@LHC in TI12/TI18.

notes: Chooz A (shut down 1991) is drawn for campus context only; the Double Chooz and NUCLEUS baselines refer to B1/B2.
Chooz A (shut down 1991) is drawn for campus context only; the Double Chooz and NUCLEUS baselines refer to B1/B2.

Source conflicts: B1-B2 separation 140 m (TDR 2006 map caption), 160 m (NUCLEUS 2019), 165 m (Double Chooz 2021), 163.3 m (OSM centroids). Far baselines 1114.6/997.9 m (TDR) vs 1115/998 m (2021); near-lab baselines 290.7/260.3 m (TDR preliminary) vs 469/355 m (2021).

The two derived positions rest on building centroids, not reactor axes, and the far-lab construction is ill-conditioned (163 m between circle centres for ~1 km radii); see the geometry records' method text.
map:chooz.summary_technical: OSM reactor-unit footprints; far laboratory and NUCLEUS VNS as derived points (two-circle intersections from published baselines with the side fixed by terrain, a neutrino-rate ratio and an OSM building); near laboratory unlocated.

notes: No accelerator or beamline entity has facility_id: facility:cjpl (it is a passive underground laboratory, not an accelerator complex), so unlocated[] has nothing to list on that front; both of the facility's sites (site:cjpl-i, site:cjpl-ii) are drawn.

detector:pandax-4t is placed at site:cjpl-ii; no independently sourced sub-position for PandaX-4T within the CJPL-II hall complex was found, so it shares geometry:cjpl-ii-point rather than getting its own feature (unlike CERN's CMS cavern point, which had its own published coordinate).
map:cjpl.summary_technical: Local map for facility:cjpl. Both halls are drawn as points derived by walking the sourced portal-to-hall distances (8.7-9.2 km) along an OpenStreetMap trace of the Jinping traffic tunnel (two near-identical parallel bores; one is drawn). The tunnel's own OSM-measured length (17.5 km) is cross-checked against the facility's published '17.5-km-long traffic tunnels' figure.

notes: Facility status is 'construction'. The approved Alpha Configuration (14 MSTs and 37 SSTs over about 3 km2, plus foundations for four LSTs and three more SSTs) defines the position of every telescope, but CTAO publishes the layout only as an unscaled figure (no scale bar, no coordinate axes) and says the released coordinates are 'as-requested', with final positions shifting by less than ten metres. No coordinate table was found on the CTAO site, the news page or the press coverage fetched on 2026-10-25, so no telescope pad is drawn.

OpenStreetMap way 939135727 ('Cherenkov Telescope Array - Southern Hemisphere Site', landuse=construction, 20 nodes, version 2, 2025-02-25; read with the OSM API map call at 2026-10-25T10:38:39Z) was considered and not drawn: it is a near-elliptical outline of 2.04 km2, 32 % smaller than the 3 km2 the array is published to cover, with its centroid 374 m from the published array coordinate, so it can be neither the array footprint nor a site boundary that contains it.
The only to-scale feature is the array's published coordinate (24d41'0.34"S, 70d18'58.84"W), good to metres as printed but a reference point of the layout, not a structure.
map:ctao-south-paranal.summary_technical: One local map for facility:ctao-south-paranal. Drawn as a single reference point at CTAO's own official published array-site coordinate; the planned telescope grid (eventually 2 LST + 14 MST + 37 SST) has no published individual pad coordinates (checked 2026-09-18).

notes: The three halls are drawn as derived points (not footprints): their positions come from multilateration, not from a survey or a tracing; accuracy_m on each hall covers the fit residual and the use of reactor-building centroids as proxies for the core centres.
map:daya-bay-reactor-neutrino-lab.summary_technical: Reactor-building footprints from OpenStreetMap (georeferenced); EH1–EH3 positions derived by least-squares multilateration from the six cores using the AD-to-core baselines of arXiv:1508.03943 Table 2 (survey uncertainty < 18 mm); overburdens from §2.2/Table 1 of the same paper.

notes: geometry:hera-halle-nord (entity_id site:desy-hera-north-hall-h1) stands in for both detector:h1 (1992-2007) and detector:alps-ii (active, in the same former HERA tunnel straight section); it is not time-sliced because sites carry no independent state_segments in this schema version, matching map:cern's documented over-display of boundary/hall features across every year.
map:desy.summary_technical: One local map for facility:desy spanning the Hamburg-Bahrenfeld campus and the full HERA ring footprint. Geometry sourced from OpenStreetMap (way 24973326 for the HERA ring; way 276641657 for the campus boundary; way 131496014 for the North Hall/H1 building; way 297515305 for the PETRA III storage-ring tunnel, drawn as context) cross-checked against DESY's own published HERA ring length and depth figures.

notes: Far sites (not drawn on this map; great-circle distances and bearings computed from the sourced site:fermilab-main-campus point): site:soudan-minos-far-detector (735.4 km, bearing 336.0 degrees, historical MINOS-era NuMI beam), site:ash-river-nova-far-detector (811.7 km, bearing 335.5 degrees, current NOvA-era NuMI beam), site:surf-4850-level-dune-far-detector (1287.6 km, bearing 287.7 degrees, LBNF beam). The Soudan and SURF sites have their own maps (map:soudan-underground-laboratory, map:surf); there is no map for the Ash River site. linked_map_ids on this map is empty.

The campus site (site:fermilab-main-campus, a 3 km point) is represented by the campus boundary and by the halls/points drawn at it with `site_id`; detectors placed there that could not be located are listed individually in `unlocated[]`.

detector:seaquest and site:fermilab-nm4-hall are drawn (geometry:fermilab-seaquest-point), from OpenStreetMap node 4425992583, tagged name=SeaQuest and addr:housenumber=NM4, inside the campus bounding box. A search of OpenStreetMap for the literal string 'NM4' finds nothing, which is why the experiment was first listed as unlocated; a search for the experiment's own name finds the node directly (checked 2026-09-21).

The Main Injector and Recycler are drawn (2026-10-25). The shape is computed from the TDR's straight-section lengths, dipole counts and lattice listing (derived; see geometry:fermilab-main-injector-ring for the derivation and the independent 28.789277 m check). The ring is placed with the TDR's own published site coordinates (Fermilab Site Coordinate System of Beams-doc-1148), accuracy 8 m; an earlier placement fitted to a road was displaced 38-74 m. The grassland polygon geometry:fermilab-mi-infield is context only.
map:fermilab.summary_technical: Local to-scale map of the Fermilab Batavia campus. Rings: a derived circle for the Booster ring (474 m sourced circumference, OSM-fit centre, with the surveyed start of the 8 GeV line as an independent check) and for the Tevatron ring (6.3 km sourced circumference, centre placed from the Main Injector design handbook's survey relation and checked against the published A0 point), and the Main Injector and Recycler as derived 3319 m rings (lattice shape from the design handbook, placed with its published site coordinates; 8 m). Detectors: georeferenced OSM building footprints for the CDF Hall, D0 Assembly Building, MINOS and NOvA near-detector surface buildings, MiniBooNE Detector Building, the LArTF/MicroBooNE hall and the Muon g-2 MC-1 building, a positionally identified ICARUS-T600 hall, an OSM-tagged point for SeaQuest/NM4 and a derived point for SBND. Beams: the NuMI target, beamlines and underground halls from the NuMI design report's beam sheet (published site coordinates); a derived BNB target and beamline anchored on two independently named OSM footprints; an approximate linac axis; and inferred-direction lines for the NuMI and LBNF beams. Context features, each drawn only from a date given or bounded by a source: the campus boundary, Wilson Hall, the MI-62 service building, MC-2 and the Main Injector grassland. PIP-II, KTeV, Mu2e, MINERvA, DONUT, SENSEI, DAMIC (prototype) and the DUNE near detector are unlocated, each with a sourced reason and backlog.

notes: Telescope positions are OpenStreetMap nodes (telescopes T1-T4, source=yahoo, edited 2026-10-08), read with the OSM API map call on 2026-10-25 because Overpass answered 502 at capacity. Their spacings agree with the labels of Figure 1 of Perkins and Maier 2009 to within 7 % (four of five labels within 4 %), and T1 is at its post-2009 position.
Buildings of the basecamp (the OSM polygons of the administrative complex and car parks) are unnamed and are not drawn; no fetched source identifies them.

Distance T1-T4 (172 m in OSM) is not in any fetched text; Figure 4 of the 2025 VERITAS overview (arXiv:2507.09813; y axis north) shows T1 about 170 m east of T4 by eye, consistent with OSM, but a figure read by eye is not cited as a source.
map:fred-lawrence-whipple-observatory.summary_technical: Four telescope points from OpenStreetMap nodes, each checked by centroid-to-centroid distance against the spacings labelled in Figure 1 of Perkins and Maier 2009 (7 % tolerance); the array outline is the quadrilateral through them with a perimeter check of 409 m (sum of the four labelled sides). Map centre is the collaboration's published array coordinate (31d40'30.21"N, 110d57'7.77"W), 24 m from the OSM quadrilateral's centroid.

notes: Telescope positions are OpenStreetMap traces (ways 171900951, 171900954, 171900955, 171900956 for the four 12 m telescopes, 171900953 for CT5), read with the OSM API map call on 2026-10-25 because Overpass answered 502 at capacity. The corner telescopes are not numbered: no fetched source says which of CT1-CT4 stands at which corner.

Other unnamed OpenStreetMap buildings stand in and around the compound; the Puhlhofer 2024 review says the site has 'multiple halls for the storage of spare parts and technical equipment' but none of these polygons is identified as such, so they are not drawn.
map:hess-khomas-highland.summary_technical: Telescope footprints from OpenStreetMap (five ways, centroid-to-centroid distances checked against the published 120 m square side and the 120 m/sqrt(2) centre-to-corner distance); the array outline is the quadrilateral through the four corner centroids, with a perimeter check of 480 m. Map centre is the collaboration's published array coordinate (23d16'18"S 16d30'00"E, good to one arc-second), which lies 21 m from the OSM CT5 centroid.

notes: No accelerator or beamline record exists for ILL; the guide halls depict facility:ill-grenoble.
The ILL's neutron guides and beam tubes between the reactor and the guide halls are not mapped in any fetched source and are not drawn.
map:ill-grenoble.summary_technical: One local map for facility:ill-grenoble. OpenStreetMap footprints (cadastre-derived): reactor building ILL 5 (way 191447189, span 59.79 m against the 60 m inner-shell diameter of an ILL engineering paper: pass), guide halls ILL 7 (way 191447188) and ILL 22 (way 191447185), and the EPN campus polygon (way 64549604). The 7 m reactor-core cylinder is a derived circle at the centre of the circular reactor building. detector:ricochet-cryocube is unlocated (distance only).

notes: No accelerator, beamline or target-station record exists for ISIS in the atlas; the R55 and R80 buildings are therefore context features attached to site:isis-rutherford-appleton by site_id, not by entity_id.
map:isis-neutron-source.summary_technical: One local map for facility:isis-neutron-source. Drawn from OpenStreetMap: the RAL campus polygon (way 69870055), building R55 (Target Station 1 experimental hall, building:part way 1454005510) and building R80 (Target Station 2, way 750266080); the R55/R80 identification is ISIS's own safety page. The synchrotron (163 m, IPAC 2014) and detector:karmen (17.7 m from the target, 100 degrees to the beam) are listed as unlocated.

notes: facility:j-parc's notes record that the Materials and Life Science Experimental Facility (MLF, fed by the RCS) and a proposed muon g-2/EDM experiment are mentioned on official J-PARC pages, but neither has an atlas accelerator/beamline/detector/experiment record of its own (out of the HEP scope this atlas models), so neither appears in this map or in `unlocated[]` -- there is no entity id to list.
map:j-parc.summary_technical: One local map for facility:j-parc covering the Tokai campus: the 400 MeV linac, 3 GeV RCS and 1567 m Main Ring tunnels (OSM indoor-mapped corridors, cross-checked against the T2K NIM paper's machine table), the Hadron Experimental Facility building (KOTO, COMET), the neutrino primary+secondary beamline tunnel and target station, the near-detector hall building (ND280, INGRID), and an inferred-direction line toward Super-Kamiokande.

notes: The CEBAF accelerator is drawn from building footprints published by the City of Newport News, in which the Jefferson Lab buildings carry the lab's own building numbers (BLDGNOTE 'Jefferson Lab #101' ...), the same numbers as the list on JLab's site plan. OpenStreetMap has no tunnel, hall or service-building outline for the lab (checked 2026-10-25 through the OSM API: 5786 ways in the box, none of them CEBAF).

The tunnel straights are the footprints of building 999 (parts 01 and 02), 265 m long; the two arcs are semicircles of 80.3 m radius fitted to the eight arc service buildings (E2-E5, W2-W5), which lie on them to within 0.6 m (W2 4.4 m). See geometry:jlab-cebaf-racetrack for the derivation and the -6.9% difference from the official 'about 7/8 of a mile'.
Site coordinate: site:jlab-newport-news (campus point 37.09896, -76.48157) is 470 m north of the racetrack centre; it is a campus-grade point and was not used as an anchor for anything.
map:jefferson-lab.summary_technical: Local map for facility:jefferson-lab. Building footprints from the City of Newport News open-data layer (lab building numbers match JLab's site plan): halls A-D (Hall A verified by a span check against the official '174 feet across'), the two 265 m building-999 strips, eleven arc/extractor/injector service buildings and 70 further buildings. geometry:jlab-cebaf-racetrack is a derived centre line: straights along the strips' axes (160.7 m apart), semicircles of 80.3 m radius fitted to the eight arc service buildings, total 1311 m against the official 'about 7/8 of a mile' (-6.9%). OSM supplies only the campus boundary and CEBAF Center.

notes: The hall was moved about 60 m north-west of its originally designed position before excavation (arXiv:2104.02565 Sec. 1.2); the CDR's overburden (728.8 m) and shaft lengths refer to the earlier design, so the 2021 figures are used for the level depth.
map:juno-jiangmen.summary_technical: Published coordinate of the hall (arXiv:2104.02565) as a surveyed point with 150 m accuracy, and the OSM outline of the surface campus. The access shafts are not drawn (no coordinates published); the Yangjiang and Taishan reactor buildings, 52-53 km from the hall, are on map:juno-reactor-baselines.

notes: Baseline statements by the collaboration: "The detector is positioned near the first maximum of the solar-driven oscillations, at an optimized distance of 52.5 km, equidistant from all reactor cores of the Yangjiang and Taishan Nuclear Power Plants (NPP)" (arXiv:2511.14593, introduction); "the experimental site is at equal distances of ∼53 km from the Yangjiang NPP and the Taishan NPP" (arXiv:2104.02565, Sec. 1.2). The surveyed per-core baselines in Table 1 of arXiv:2104.02565 span 52.11 to 52.82 km, so the equal-distance figure is nominal. Checked 2026-10-25.

Core numbering YJ-1..6 / TS-1..2 is assigned by matching the order of the measured distances to the order of the published baselines; the OSM ways carry no unit numbers. The Taishan EPR units 3 and 4 (baselines 52.32 and 52.20 km in the CDR) were not built; arXiv:2104.02565 says only that two more cores 'possibly' may be built.
Far reactors: arXiv:2104.02565 Sec. 1.2 puts the Daya Bay complex 215 km (and Huizhou 265 km) from the detector, beyond a local map; Daya Bay has its own map (linked).

Residual: the six Yangjiang buildings are all 96-101 m farther from the published hall coordinate than the surveyed baselines say, the Taishan buildings agree to <= 16 m. The sign pattern is that of a ~100 m displacement of the published coordinate toward SSW, or of an OSM registration offset between the two plants; the sources cannot separate them.
map:juno-reactor-baselines.summary_technical: Published hall coordinate (arXiv:2104.02565, Sec. 1.2) and OSM reactor buildings of Yangjiang (six building=reactor ways) and Taishan (two nuclear-island buildings). Each building's centroid-to-hall distance is checked at 0.3 % tolerance against the GPS-surveyed core baselines of arXiv:2104.02565 Table 1 (YJ-1 to YJ-6: 52.74, 52.82, 52.41, 52.49, 52.11, 52.19 km; TS-1, TS-2: 52.77, 52.64 km; surveyed to 1 m). The JUNO Collaboration gives the nominal baseline as 52.5 km (arXiv:2511.14593, introduction) and as about 53 km (arXiv:2104.02565, Sec. 1.2). No baseline lines or distance labels are drawn. Companion to map:juno-jiangmen.

notes: facility:kamioka-observatory's own notes record that the Kamioka Observatory also hosts KAGRA, CANDLES, NEWAGE and XENONnT R&D, and that experiment:kamiokande/experiment:kamland-zen exist as atlas experiment records; none of these have their own site: record in this atlas (only the two mines already in site_ids do), so there is nothing further to draw or list in unlocated[] for them — flagged here as a completeness gap, not a map defect.

The only OpenStreetMap results for the Mozumi area are one named mine-entrance node and one mountain-summit survey point (geometry:kamioka-mine-entrance, geometry:ikenoyama-peak-marker), obtained through the fallback Overpass mirror maps.mail.ru. No ICRR surface-building footprints were found, and the Atotsu entrance cannot be told apart from the Mozumi entrance. A named-building query (`way["building"]["name"]`) over a wider bounding box on maps.mail.ru or overpass.private.coffee, or fetching a known building way directly via https://api.openstreetmap.org/api/0.6/way/<id>/full.json once one is identified, would settle whether ICRR buildings are mapped.
map:kamioka-observatory.summary_technical: Local map for facility:kamioka-observatory spanning the Mozumi mine (site:kamioka-mozumi-mine-super-kamiokande, site:kamioka-kamland) and the Tochibora mine (site:kamioka-hyper-kamiokande-tochibora), 8 km apart. Super-Kamiokande is drawn as a derived 39.3 m circle around its own surveyed GPS centre; Hyper-Kamiokande as a surveyed point from its 2011 Letter of Intent; KamLAND as the coarse point already on record (no better source was found). An inferred_direction feature shows the T2K beam's 295 km baseline from J-PARC, cross-checked against the T2K instrumentation paper's own surveyed figure.

notes: accelerator:kek-ps is drawn (geometry:kek-north-counter-hall) rather than listed as not drawn, but the identification is circumstantial and marked as such; see that record's own notes. No source found gives the 12 GeV PS ring's own tunnel path; two targeted Overpass searches for tunnel/particle_accelerator/landuse ways near the historic PS site found none.
map:kek.summary_technical: One local map for facility:kek covering the Tsukuba campus: the 3016 m KEKB/SuperKEKB ring tunnel (OSM way 138322704, cross-checked against the SuperKEKB accelerator paper's own machine-parameter table), the Tsukuba interaction hall (Belle, Belle II) and the ring's Oho/Fuji/Nikko straight-section halls, the KEK injector linac building, a building tentatively identified with the historic KEK-PS North Counter Hall, and an inferred-direction line for the K2K beam toward Super-Kamiokande.

notes: No accelerator or beamline record exists for KIT in the atlas, so the KATRIN setup is represented by detector:katrin (outline) and the beamline is listed as unlocated against the facility.
The building used for KATRIN, OSM way 394890935, was found through an OpenStreetMap API bounding-box read; a Nominatim search cannot find it because Nominatim does not search by tag.

The beam axis and the main spectrometer vessel are drawn as derived shapes; their direction and spacing are sourced, their position inside the hall is bounded by constraints (accuracy 20 m), as described in each record.
map:kit-karlsruhe.summary_technical: Local map for facility:kit-karlsruhe. Drawn from OpenStreetMap: the campus polygon (way 155843597), the KATRIN outline (way 394890935) and Tritium Laboratory buildings 451 and 452. Derived (accuracy 20 m): the KATRIN beam axis from the WGTS coil centre (z = -38.87 m) to the detector coil centre (+13.78 m) at bearing 16 deg, and the main spectrometer vessel footprint (23.23 m x 9.8 m), using Table 1 of Glueck et al. 2013, the 16 deg orientation of the KATRIN Collaboration and the constraint that the vessel and detector lie in the outline and the WGTS in building 452. Not drawn: the rear section, the detector end, the monitor spectrometer.

notes: Portopalo di Capo Passero, the nearest shore town, is ~100 km from this site (per the KM3NeT-It page and the Letter of Intent), more than the 60 km limit for drawing a shore feature as context on the same map. It is not drawn here, and there is no separate Atlas facility or site record for it to anchor a linked map either.
A sea site has no OpenStreetMap features to draw, so none are drawn.
map:km3net-arca.summary_technical: Local map for the KM3NeT-It / ARCA deep-sea site (facility:km3net). One surveyed point (the collaboration's own published 36°16' N 16°06' E) and one derived ~1 km-diameter circle for a single ARCA building block (R=500 m per the KM3NeT 2.0 Letter of Intent). ARCA and ORCA are ~900 km apart and cannot share a to-scale map; see map:km3net-orca (linked).
